This week’s security news is mostly about weak spots. Browsers, bots, sandboxes, AI systems, and email flows all show the same problem in different ways. Everything looks normal until someone tests a small gap and finds a way through. This is not one big break. It is small permissions, weak checks, open systems, and normal tools doing things they were allowed to do. That same pattern runs

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Platform-aware phishing: ConnectWise/ScreenConnect or Itarian RAT dropped via browser download (Cofense) · [LLM] Fake-INTERPOL law-enforcement phishing with Proton Drive payload link · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ThreatsDay: AI Compute Hijacking, Apple Email Flaw, BlueHammer Ransomware + 14 S
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] BeepRAT dropper HFY.exe spawning cmd/PowerShell (China-nexus DCRat variant) · [LLM] BeepRAT scheduled-task persistence for user-writable / app-directory binary · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] BeepRAT DoH C2 bootstrap to api.service.bio / public DoH resolvers from non-browser process · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
BeepRAT dropper HFY.exe spawning cmd/PowerShell (China-nexus DCRat variant) AIInstallation High
Hunts the .NET telephone-utility dropper HFY.exe (bundled in a trojanized ZIP) launching interactive cmd.exe or powershell.exe as part of the BeepRAT multi-stage chain reported by Rubrik Zero Labs. The parent binary name is the article-specific anchor; a purported phone-number tool spawning a shell is not legitimate behaviour. Rationale: Anchored on the article's named dropper 'HFY.exe' (a .NET app masquerading as a Chinese phone-number management tool) as parent of a shell — a hard behavioural contradiction. DCRat family corroborated via Malpedia/Fortinet; BeepRAT is the article-specific customized variant. Cross-checked against: • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.dcrat • https://www.fortinet.com/blog/threat-research/dcrat-impersonating-the-columbian-government • https://zerolabs.rubrik.com/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.003 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An unrelated legitimate app also named HFY.exe in a niche telephony deployment launching a maintenance script
  • IT packaging/testing of the sample in a detonation VM
  • Security researcher manually detonating the ZIP on an analysis host
  • EDR replaying a quarantined-then-restored sample
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\") and InitiatingProcessSHA256 in (dynamic([])))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull HFY.exe SHA256 and folder path; confirm it sits in a ZIP-extract / Downloads / user-writable dir and is unsigned or self-signed. Check the child cmd/PowerShell command line for staging or DoH bootstrap. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the HFY.exe process tree, and quarantine the binary and its bundled DB-driver DLLs. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for schtasks.exe persistence (UC2), DoH beacons to api.service.bio / public DoH resolvers (UC3), and in-memory .NET assembly loads.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "HFY.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\HFY.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine

BeepRAT scheduled-task persistence for user-writable / app-directory binary AIInstallation Medium
Hunts schtasks.exe /create invocations whose task action points at HFY.exe or a binary in a user-writable path (AppData, Temp, Public, user profile) — the persistence step Rubrik describes for BeepRAT. Scoped to interactive (non-machine) accounts to cut SYSTEM/installer noise. Rationale: Uses the article's persistence claim ('establishes persistence via scheduled tasks') plus the named dropper HFY.exe and user-writable paths (where BeepRAT lives) to distinguish malicious autoruns from admin/software-installer task creation. Cross-checked against: • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.dcrat • https://zerolabs.rubrik.com/
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate software installers/updaters registering per-user tasks under AppData (Teams, OneDrive, Chrome updater)
  • Backup or sync agents scheduling tasks from a Temp staging path
  • Login-script or MDM tooling creating user-profile tasks
  • Developer tooling scheduling build jobs from a project folder under the user profile
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("onedrivesetup.exe","update.exe","teams.exe","googleupdate.exe","setup.exe","msiexec.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the task name and the target binary path/args from the command line; verify signature and reputation of the referenced .exe. Cross-check whether the same host ran HFY.exe (UC1). 2) Contain: delete the malicious scheduled task (schtasks /delete), quarantine the target binary, isolate if BeepRAT-linked. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for identical task names/paths and for DoH C2 (UC3); review other autoruns (Run keys, services) created by the same account in the window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("HFY.exe", @"\AppData\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\Temp\", @"\Roaming\")
| where AccountName !endswith "$" and AccountName !in~ ("system","local service","network service")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create"
| where CommandLine has_any ("HFY.exe", "\\AppData\\", "\\Users\\Public\\", "\\Temp\\", "\\Roaming\\")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
title: Scheduled Task Registered for User-Writable Binary (BeepRAT)

detection:

      - '\AppData\'

  condition: selection and paths
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\schtasks.exe OR *\SCHTASKS.EXE) @CommandLine:(*create* OR *CREATE*) @CommandLine:(*HFY.exe* OR *\AppData\* OR *\Users\Public\* OR *\Temp\* OR *\Roaming\*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\schtasks\.exe$/i
| regex("/create", field=CommandLine, flags=i)
| regex("(HFY\.exe|\\\\AppData\\\\|\\\\Users\\\\Public\\\\|\\\\Temp\\\\|\\\\Roaming\\\\)", field=CommandLine, flags=i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*" AND (Processes.process="*HFY.exe*" OR Processes.process="*\\AppData\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Users\\Public\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Temp\\*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | search NOT user IN ("*$","SYSTEM","LOCAL SERVICE","NETWORK SERVICE") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*" AND (Processes.process="*HFY.exe*" OR Processes.process="*\\AppData\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Users\\Public\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Temp\\*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | search NOT user IN ("*$","SYSTEM","LOCAL SERVICE","NETWORK SERVICE") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
BeepRAT DoH C2 bootstrap to api.service.bio / public DoH resolvers from non-browser process AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts endpoint-originated DNS-over-HTTPS traffic to public DoH resolvers or the campaign domain api.service.bio initiated by a process that is NOT a browser — the network-filter-evasion technique BeepRAT uses to resolve and beacon to its C2. Non-browser DoH is a strong anomaly. Rationale: Combines the article's evasion detail ('resolves C2 using DNS-over-HTTPS') with the extracted campaign domain api.service.bio and a non-browser-process filter. Note: api.service.bio is single-sourced (article extraction only) so it is one selector among behavioural resolver anchors, not the sole signal. Cross-checked against: • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.dcrat • https://zerolabs.rubrik.com/
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1132.001 T1105
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security/privacy agents (NextDNS client, Cloudflare WARP, some AV) legitimately using DoH from a non-browser service
  • Enterprise-approved DoH forwarder or Windows built-in DoH via svchost
  • Developer tools/curl scripts testing DoH endpoints
  • IoT/updater agents that resolve over DoH by design
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("warp-svc.exe","cloudflared.exe","nextdns.exe","svchost.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Program Files\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and path; is it HFY.exe or another user-writable binary (UC1)? Confirm the destination is a DoH endpoint or api.service.bio and not an approved corporate resolver. 2) Contain: block api.service.bio and rogue DoH resolvers at egress, isolate the host, capture memory (in-memory .NET assemblies expected). 3) Hunt: correlate to schtasks persistence (UC2) and process/drive/netstat enumeration bursts; sweep fleet for the same non-browser process contacting DoH.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("cloudflare-dns.com","mozilla.cloudflare-dns.com","dns.google","dns.quad9.net","doh.opendns.com","dns.nextdns.io") or RemoteUrl =~ "api.service.bio"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe","arc.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has_any ("cloudflare-dns.com","mozilla.cloudflare-dns.com","dns.google","dns.quad9.net","doh.opendns.com","dns.nextdns.io") or DstHostname =~ "api.service.bio"
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "Mozilla" or isempty(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, DstHostname, DstIpAddr, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent

Platform-aware phishing: ConnectWise/ScreenConnect or Itarian RAT dropped via browser download (Cofense) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts signed remote-access tooling (ConnectWise Control / ScreenConnect, Itarian/Comodo RMM) or the Ninite loader executing from a browser download, Temp, or AppData path — the Windows payload arm of the Cofense-reported User-Agent-fingerprinting campaign. Legitimate RMM binaries arriving via a user's browser to an endpoint that isn't managed by that RMM are high-signal. Rationale: Uses the Cofense campaign's named payloads (Itarian RAT, ConnectWise/ScreenConnect, Ninite Loader) plus a browser-parent + user-writable-path pivot to separate weaponized RMM delivery from IT-sanctioned installs. Corroborated directly by Cofense and Dark Reading. Cross-checked against: • https://cofense.com/blog/the-platform-you-trust-is-the-platform-they-target • https://www.darkreading.com/application-security/phishing-campaigns-auto-adapt-victims-device-os • https://www.bankinfosecurity.com/attackers-wield-signed-connectwise-installers-as-malware-a-28799
ATT&CKT1219 T1204.002 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • MSP/helpdesk legitimately having the user download and run a ConnectWise/ScreenConnect support session client
  • Sanctioned Ninite bulk-installer runs by IT from a Downloads folder
  • Comodo/Itarian being the org's actual endpoint-management product
  • Self-service software-portal downloads that stage installers in Temp
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("support.mycompany","rmm.mycompany") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the RMM tool is the org's sanctioned product and whether the download originated from an emailed/phished link; inspect the ScreenConnect relay/instance URL in the command line (attacker instances differ from corporate). 2) Contain: terminate the RMM client, block the attacker relay domain, and revoke any established remote session; isolate if unsanctioned. 3) Hunt: review the source email/URL (User-Agent fingerprinting redirect), check for macOS/Android credential-phish siblings for the same recipient, and sweep for the same RMM instance ID across hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","explorer.exe","outlook.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe","Ninite.exe","NiniteOne.exe","ITSMService.exe","RmmService.exe","ITSMAgent.exe")
    or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has_any ("ScreenConnect","ConnectWise Control","Itarian","Comodo")
    or FolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\") or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has_any ("ScreenConnect","ConnectWise Control","Itarian","Comodo")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","explorer.exe","outlook.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("ScreenConnect","ConnectWiseControl","Ninite","ITSMService.exe","RmmService.exe","ITSMAgent.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\Downloads\\","\\Temp\\","\\AppData\\") or NewProcessName has_any ("ScreenConnect","ConnectWiseControl")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
title: Remote Access Tool or Ninite Loader Launched From Browser Download

Fake-INTERPOL law-enforcement phishing with Proton Drive payload link AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound emails impersonating INTERPOL/law-enforcement 'investigation' notices that carry a link to Proton Drive (where the password-protected archive delivering custom ransomware is hosted), per Bitdefender. Combines lure-subject language with the Proton Drive delivery domain to keep it campaign-specific. Rationale: Pairs the Bitdefender-reported lure semantics (fake INTERPOL/law-enforcement investigation emails pressuring recipients) with the specific Proton Drive hosting domain used to stage the archive → custom ransomware, avoiding a generic 'inbound phishing' template. Sentinel/Datadog/Falcon left empty: no M365 mailflow table exists in this tenant's Sentinel schema, and FDR/CloudWatch don't ship O365 email. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/threatsday-ai-compute-hijacking-apple.html
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1204.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate correspondence from a genuine law-enforcement liaison referencing an investigation
  • A partner legitimately sharing files via Proton Drive to your users
  • Security-awareness phishing-simulation emails using law-enforcement themes
  • Journalists/legal teams that routinely receive investigation-related mail and Proton links
Suppression filter
| where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm sender authenticity (SPF/DKIM/DMARC in AuthenticationDetails), inspect the Proton Drive URL and whether recipients clicked (UrlClickEvents); check for a password-protected archive attachment. 2) Contain: soft-delete/quarantine the message across all recipients, block the Proton Drive URL and sender, and warn recipients not to open the archive. 3) Hunt: if any recipient executed the payload, pivot to endpoint for rapid mass file rename + ransom-note creation and unusual archive-extraction → new-process chains from Downloads.
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let LureMail = EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
    | where Subject has_any ("INTERPOL","Interpol","investigation","suspicious activity","law enforcement","police","evidence","legal notice")
    | project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderDisplayName, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, AttachmentCount;
LureMail
| join kind=inner (
    EmailUrlInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where UrlDomain has_any ("proton.me","drive.proton.me","pd.proton.me","protondrive")
    | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderDisplayName, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url, UrlDomain, DeliveryAction, AttachmentCount
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let LureMail = EmailEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
    | where Subject has_any ("INTERPOL","Interpol","investigation","suspicious activity","law enforcement","police","evidence","legal notice")
    | project TimeGenerated, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderDisplayName, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, AttachmentCount;
LureMail
| join kind=inner (
    EmailUrlInfo
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where UrlDomain has_any ("proton.me","drive.proton.me","pd.proton.me","protondrive")
    | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project TimeGenerated, SenderFromAddress, SenderDisplayName, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url, UrlDomain, DeliveryAction, AttachmentCount
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")

External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.

Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

10 Layers Deep: How StepSecurity Stops TeamPCP's Trivy Supply Chain Attack on GitHub Actions

StepSecurity
2026-07-02 6 use cases 3 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

TeamPCP weaponized 76 Trivy version tags overnight. The KICS attack followed the same playbook days later. One security control is not enough. Here is how the StepSecurity platform's ten independent security layers work together to prevent credential exfiltration, detect compromised actions at runtime, and respond to incidents across your entire organization before attackers can succeed.

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Egress to TeamPCP Trivy C2 (scan.aquasecurtiy.org / 45.148.10.212 + Cloudflare-tunnel fallback) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] TeamPCP trivy-action stealer reading Runner.Worker memory via /proc/<pid>/mem
TeamPCP trivy-action stealer reading Runner.Worker memory via /proc/<pid>/mem AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts a process reading another process's memory through the /proc/<pid>/mem interface — the exact technique the trojanized aquasecurity/trivy-action (CVE-2026-33634) used to scrape CI/CD secrets and environment variables out of the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker process on self-hosted/ARC runners. Article-specific because explicit /proc/<numeric>/mem reads by a CI-runner child are rare and high-fidelity, unlike generic credential-dumping templates. Rationale: Anchors on the article's verbatim /proc/pid/mem code block and the Runner.Worker memory-read behaviour; Microsoft, CrowdStrike and Aqua all confirm the stealer read GitHub Actions runner-worker memory to harvest secrets. Explicit /proc/<pid>/mem reads outside debuggers are a rare, high-fidelity credential-access signal (T1003.007). Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/03/24/detecting-investigating-defending-against-trivy-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/from-scanner-to-stealer-inside-the-trivy-action-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.aquasec.com/blog/trivy-supply-chain-attack-what-you-need-to-know/ • https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy/security/advisories/GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23
ATT&CKT1003.007 T1552.001 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer/SRE debugging with gdb, lldb or gcore attaching to a live process on a build host
  • CRIU checkpoint/restore of containers reading process memory during live migration
  • Performance profilers or crash-dump handlers (ABRT, systemd-coredump helpers) touching /proc/<pid>/mem
  • Legitimate memory-forensics or security tooling (e.g. Volatility acquisition helpers) run by the blue team
  • Custom in-house observability agents that read /proc/<pid>/mem for heap inspection
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("gdb","lldb","strace","criu","gcore") or FileName in~ ("gdb","lldb","strace","criu","gcore","systemd-coredump"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree — confirm the reader's parent chain traces to an actions-runner / Runner.Worker / trivy-action job and that the target PID is Runner.Worker. Capture the reader's command line and SHA256. 2) Contain: isolate/terminate the runner (ARC lockdown or stop the VM), revoke and rotate every secret and cloud token (AWS/GCP/Azure/Kubernetes/Git) that was in the job scope — assume exfiltration. 3) Hunt: search the org for repos named tpcp-docs, review which repos reference aquasecurity/trivy-action or setup-trivy by mutable tag, and pivot to UC2 for egress to scan.aquasecurtiy.org / the C2 IPs from the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/proc/[0-9]+/mem"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where not(FileName in~ ("gdb","lldb","strace","criu","gcore","dumpcap"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentProc = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RunnerContext = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/proc/[0-9]+/mem"
   or TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/proc/[0-9]+/mem"
| where not(ActingProcessName in~ ("gdb","lldb","strace","criu","gcore"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          ProcName = ActingProcessName,
          Cmd = ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: TeamPCP Trivy Stealer Reading Runner.Worker Memory via /proc/pid/mem
id: 7b3d9c14-2a6e-4f81-9c0a-5d21e8b4f6a2
status: experimental
description: Detects a process reading another process's memory through /proc/<pid>/mem, the technique the trojanized aquasecurity/trivy-action (CVE-2026-33634, TeamPCP) used to scrape CI/CD secrets from the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker process.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/10-layers-deep-how-stepsecurity-stops-teampcps-trivy-supply-chain-attack-on-github-actions
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/03/24/detecting-investigating-defending-against-trivy-supply-chain-compromise/
  - https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/from-scanner-to-stealer-inside-the-trivy-action-supply-chain-compromise/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/02
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1003.007
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    CommandLine|re: '/proc/[0-9]+/mem'
  filter_debug:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/gdb'
      - '/lldb'
      - '/strace'
      - '/criu'
      - '/gcore'
  condition: selection and not filter_debug
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.command_line:*/proc/* AND @process.command_line:*/mem*) -@process.executable.path:(*/gdb OR */lldb OR */strace OR */criu OR */gcore)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 event_platform=Lin
| regex("/proc/\d+/mem", field=CommandLine)
| NOT ImageFileName=/\/(gdb|lldb|strace|criu|gcore)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*/proc/*/mem*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | regex process="/proc/[0-9]+/mem" | search NOT process_name IN ("gdb","lldb","strace","criu","gcore") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*/proc/*/mem*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | regex process="/proc/[0-9]+/mem" | search NOT process_name IN ("gdb","lldb","strace","criu","gcore") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Egress to TeamPCP Trivy C2 (scan.aquasecurtiy.org / 45.148.10.212 + Cloudflare-tunnel fallback) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts DNS resolution or network connections to the TeamPCP exfiltration infrastructure used by the compromised aquasecurity/trivy-action and setup-trivy actions: the typosquat scan.aquasecurtiy.org (45.148.10.212, Amsterdam), the confirmed C2 IPs, and the corroborated Cloudflare-tunnel fallback plug-tab-protective-relay.trycloudflare.com. Article-specific hard IOCs; any hit means stolen CI/CD secrets left the runner. Rationale: Uses the article's verbatim exfil domain scan.aquasecurtiy.org and its resolved IP 45.148.10.212 plus the two additional TeamPCP IPs, enriched with the Cloudflare-tunnel fallback (plug-tab-protective-relay.trycloudflare.com) confirmed by Aqua and StepSecurity's second write-up. All are hard IOCs - any resolution/connection is a confirmed exfiltration of CI/CD secrets. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/trivy-compromised-teampcp-supply-chain-attack • https://www.aquasec.com/blog/trivy-supply-chain-attack-what-you-need-to-know/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/trivy-compromised-a-second-time---malicious-v0-69-4-release • https://thehackernews.com/2026/03/trivy-security-scanner-github-actions.html
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1071.001 T1568.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher or blue-teamer deliberately resolving the IOC domains during investigation from a sandbox host
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling / passive DNS pipelines that query indicator domains for validation
  • A legitimate but unrelated Cloudflare tunnel in use by dev teams sharing the *.trycloudflare.com parent (only the exact host plug-tab-protective-relay.trycloudflare.com is malicious)
  • Proxy/sinkhole appliance that answers the typosquat domain and generates a benign-looking connection log
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host/runner and the initiating process — confirm it is a CI runner running trivy-action/setup-trivy, and pull the time window against UC1 for the preceding /proc/<pid>/mem read. 2) Contain: block scan.aquasecurtiy.org, plug-tab-protective-relay.trycloudflare.com and 45.148.10.212 / 83.142.209.203 / 94.154.172.43 at the egress proxy/firewall; isolate the runner and treat all job-scoped secrets as compromised — rotate immediately. 3) Hunt: enumerate every repo referencing aquasecurity/trivy-action or setup-trivy by mutable tag, search the GitHub org for tpcp-docs repos (successful-exfil marker), and review cloud audit logs (CloudTrail/Entra/GCP) for use of the leaked tokens from unfamiliar IPs.
let c2Domains = dynamic(["scan.aquasecurtiy.org","plug-tab-protective-relay.trycloudflare.com"]);
let c2IPs = dynamic(["45.148.10.212","83.142.209.203","94.154.172.43"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl in~ (c2Domains) or RemoteIP in (c2IPs)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2IPs = dynamic(["45.148.10.212","83.142.209.203","94.154.172.43"]);
let c2Domains = dynamic(["scan.aquasecurtiy.org","plug-tab-protective-relay.trycloudflare.com"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImDnsActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DnsQuery in~ (c2Domains)
    | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, Host = DvcHostname, Indicator = DnsQuery, Kind = "dns"),
  (ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DstIpAddr in (c2IPs)
    | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, Host = DstHostname, Indicator = DstIpAddr, Kind = "network")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"

| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33634")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33634")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"

| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'

        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'

      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

ConsentFix and ClickFix: How Microsoft 365 Accounts are Hijacked in 3 Seconds

BleepingComputer
2026-07-02 14 use cases 6 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

ConsentFix and ClickFix attacks steal Microsoft 365 tokens in seconds using fake prompts and OAuth flows. Learn how these MFA bypass tactics work and how to defend against them. [...]

ATT&CKT1059.001 T1190 T1204.004 T1486 T1528 T1566
Domainssecurity-updater.com

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ConsentFix/ClickFix phishing-page callouts to named lookalike M365 domains · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] ClickFix payload fetch: LOLBin command line referencing campaign phishing domains · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] ConsentFix: Azure CLI OAuth token replay from campaign IPs (MFA bypass) · [LLM] ConsentFix post-compromise mailbox access & inbox-rule creation from campaign IPs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
ConsentFix/ClickFix phishing-page callouts to named lookalike M365 domains AIDelivery High
Hunts endpoint browser navigation and DNS resolution to the three dedicated phishing domains that host the spoofed Microsoft sign-in / fake-verification pages in this campaign. Article-specific because it keys on the exact domains, not a generic 'newly-seen domain' heuristic. Rationale: Uses the three exact campaign domains (trustpointassurance.com, fastwaycheck.com, previewcentral.com) from the article's IOC set, scoped to browser/Outlook-initiated traffic to cut noise. Dedicated phishing infra means any resolution is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://pushsecurity.com/blog/consentfix • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4105230/meet-consentfix-a-new-twist-on-the-clickfix-phishing-attack.html
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or SOC analyst manually detonating the lure in a sandbox from a corporate host
  • Threat-intel/URL-scanning tooling (urlscan.io, VirusTotal retro-hunt) resolving the domain from an on-prem collector
  • A legitimately re-registered/parked domain if the phishing infra is later sinkholed and reused
  • Automated Safe-Links detonation appliance resolving the domain on the user's behalf
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the DeviceName/user and confirm whether the browser actually loaded a page (RemoteUrl full path, HTTP 200) vs a passive resolution; pull UrlClickEvents for the same user. 2) Contain: block the three domains at proxy/DNS, revoke the user's active M365 sessions and reset tokens if the page was reached. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same user's Azure CLI (AppId 04b07795-...) sign-ins and OfficeActivity MailItemsAccessed from unusual IPs (see credential-access and collection UCs) to confirm token theft.
let PhishDomains = dynamic(["trustpointassurance.com","fastwaycheck.com","previewcentral.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (PhishDomains)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe","outlook.exe","olk.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let PhishDomains = dynamic(["trustpointassurance.com","fastwaycheck.com","previewcentral.com"]);
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any (PhishDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ConsentFix/ClickFix phishing domain DNS resolution
id: 6f2a4b9e-3c71-4d2a-9e58-7b1c4f9a2d10
description: DNS query for the dedicated phishing domains hosting the ConsentFix/ClickFix spoofed Microsoft sign-in pages
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/consentfix-and-clickfix-how-microsoft-365-accounts-are-hijacked-in-3-seconds/
  - https://pushsecurity.com/blog/consentfix
author: SOC Detection Engineering

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*trustpointassurance.com*" OR Web.url="*fastwaycheck.com*" OR Web.url="*previewcentral.com*" OR Web.dest="trustpointassurance.com" OR Web.dest="fastwaycheck.com" OR Web.dest="previewcentral.com") by Web.src Web.user Web.dest Web.url Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*trustpointassurance.com*" OR Web.url="*fastwaycheck.com*" OR Web.url="*previewcentral.com*" OR Web.dest="trustpointassurance.com" OR Web.dest="fastwaycheck.com" OR Web.dest="previewcentral.com") by Web.src Web.user Web.dest Web.url Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
ClickFix payload fetch: LOLBin command line referencing campaign phishing domains AIExploitation High
Hunts the ClickFix execution leg where the pasted command (run via a LOLBin such as PowerShell/mshta/curl/certutil) reaches out to one of the campaign's named domains to pull the next stage. Distinct from generic encoded-PowerShell rules because it keys on the specific domains in the command line. Rationale: Combines the article's ClickFix execution behaviour (interpreter/LOLBin spawned to run pasted commands) with the exact campaign domains in the command line, making it far higher fidelity than a bare PowerShell rule and non-overlapping with the excluded encoded-PowerShell detection. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/advanced-phishing-tradecraft • https://pushsecurity.com/blog/consentfix
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin script or monitoring tool that legitimately curls one of these hostnames (unlikely given they are phishing infra, but possible after domain re-registration)
  • Threat-hunt/IR analyst copy-pasting the IOC into a test command on a corporate host
  • EDR/AV retro-scan tooling passing the domain string as an argument
  • Security-awareness phishing-simulation platform replaying the payload
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MpCmdRun.exe") and AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full ProcessCommandLine and parent (InitiatingProcessFileName) — an explorer.exe or browser parent confirms the ClickFix Run-dialog/paste vector; note SHA256 of any downloaded stage. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process tree, block the domains, and revoke the signed-in user's M365 tokens. 3) Hunt: sweep for the fetched second stage across other hosts and check the same user's Azure CLI sign-ins and mailbox access from the campaign IPs.
let PhishDomains = dynamic(["trustpointassurance.com","fastwaycheck.com","previewcentral.com"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (PhishDomains)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let PhishDomains = dynamic(["trustpointassurance.com","fastwaycheck.com","previewcentral.com"]);
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any (PhishDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ConsentFix: Azure CLI OAuth token replay from campaign IPs (MFA bypass) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the ConsentFix payoff — the attacker exchanging/replaying the stolen Azure CLI OAuth authorization code, appearing as sign-ins to the Microsoft Azure CLI first-party app (AppId 04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46) from the campaign source IPs with no interactive MFA. This is the flagship, passwordless, MFA-bypassing account-takeover signal. Rationale: Grounds the article's OAuth-token-theft claim in the corroborated real-world mechanism (Push Security/Mitiga): ConsentFix abuses the Microsoft Azure CLI public client (AppId 04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46). Pairing that app with the article's three source IPs yields a passwordless-ATO alert with near-zero FPs. Cross-checked against: • https://pushsecurity.com/blog/consentfix • https://www.mitiga.io/blog/consentfix-oauth-phishing-explained-how-token-based-attacks-bypass-mfa-in-microsoft-entra-id • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/new-attack-technique-consentfix-hijacks-oauth-consent-grants/
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer/DevOps engineer legitimately running `az login` from a VPN egress that happens to overlap the flagged range (verify user is a known Azure operator)
  • CI/CD runner or automation using Azure CLI from a cloud egress IP
  • Penetration-test or purple-team exercise replaying the ConsentFix flow with authorization
  • Shared NAT/proxy IP where a benign Azure CLI session coincidentally shares the address
Suppression filter
| where AccountUpn !in~ ("svc-azuredevops@contoso.com") and not (ClientAppUsed == "Mobile Apps and Desktop clients" and AuthenticationRequirement == "multiFactorAuthentication")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the UPN is not a routine Azure CLI user and that the sign-in shows non-interactive / no fresh MFA (AuthenticationRequirement, IsInteractive); pull the geo/ASN of the IP. 2) Contain: immediately revoke refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession / 'Revoke sessions'), disable the account, and require re-auth with a compliant device. 3) Hunt: enumerate all activity from the token — OfficeActivity MailItemsAccessed, new inbox rules, OAuth app grants, and any downstream Azure/Graph calls from the same IPs (see collection UC).
let CampaignIPs = dynamic(["12.75.216.90","182.3.36.223","12.75.116.137"]);
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ApplicationId == "04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46"   // Microsoft Azure CLI first-party app abused by ConsentFix
| where IPAddress in (CampaignIPs)
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Application, ApplicationId, IPAddress, Country, City, IsInteractive, AuthenticationRequirement, ClientAppUsed, ErrorCode, RiskLevelDuringSignIn
| order by Timestamp desc
let CampaignIPs = dynamic(["12.75.216.90","182.3.36.223","12.75.116.137"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where AppId == "04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46" | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppId, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, Location, ResultType, ClientAppUsed, AuthenticationRequirement),
  (AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where AppId == "04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46" | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppId, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, Location, ResultType, ClientAppUsed, AuthenticationRequirement)
| where IPAddress in (CampaignIPs)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ConsentFix post-compromise mailbox access & inbox-rule creation from campaign IPs AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the collection stage where the stolen session reads the victim mailbox or plants inbox rules, seen as MailItemsAccessed / New-InboxRule operations sourced from the three campaign IPs. Confirms the token theft translated into hands-on-keyboard mailbox abuse. Rationale: Uses the article's collection behaviour (session-based mailbox read / inbox-rule abuse) anchored to the three campaign IPs on Exchange audit operations. IP-scoped mailbox-access + rule-creation is a clean, low-FP confirmation that the ConsentFix token was actioned. Cross-checked against: • https://pushsecurity.com/blog/consentfix • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4105230/meet-consentfix-a-new-twist-on-the-clickfix-phishing-attack.html
ATT&CKT1114.002 T1550.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate user working from an IP that happens to fall in the same range (verify against the user's baseline logon locations)
  • eDiscovery/compliance tool or delegated admin accessing the mailbox from a datacenter IP
  • Mobile-device mail sync via a carrier NAT overlapping the address
  • Authorized mailbox migration/backup service performing bulk reads
Suppression filter
| where UserId !endswith "onmicrosoft.com" or ClientInfoString !has "eDiscovery"
Response runbook
1) Triage: list every Operation from the campaign IP for the affected UserId — MailItemsAccessed volume, any New-InboxRule that forwards/deletes, and the mailbox items touched. 2) Contain: revoke sessions/tokens, delete malicious inbox rules, block the IPs at Conditional Access, and force password + MFA re-registration. 3) Hunt: check for outbound BEC (sent items, external forwarding), OAuth app grants added during the session, and the same IPs touching other mailboxes in the tenant.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc
