ToddyCat-Linked Umbrij Malware Abuses OAuth to Access Gmail via Google API

The Hacker News
2026-07-02 14 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The threat actor known as ToddyCat has been attributed to a new malware called Umbrij that's designed to gain surreptitious access to a victim's email correspondence via the Google API. "In this campaign, the attackers focused their attention on corporate email communications hosted on Gmail, targeting access compromise via APIs," Kaspersky said in a detailed report published this week. "

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ToddyCat-Linked Umbrij Malware Abuses OAuth to Access Gmail via Google API
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] ToddyCat Umbrij DLL side-load host (BDSubWiz/VSTestVideoRecorder/GoogleDesktop) run from anomalous path · [LLM] Scheduled task impersonating Kaspersky EDR (KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp) to launch signed side-load host · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Chromium headless remote-debugging launch against copied BackupFiles profile (STRD OAuth token theft) · [LLM] Umbrij copies Chrome/Edge credential stores into %LOCALAPPDATA%\...\BackupFiles · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
ToddyCat Umbrij DLL side-load host (BDSubWiz/VSTestVideoRecorder/GoogleDesktop) run from anomalous path AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution of the three legitimate signed binaries ToddyCat abuses to side-load the ConfuserEx-obfuscated Umbrij .NET DLL, filtered to executions outside each binary's genuine vendor install directory. GoogleDesktop.exe is a discontinued product and VSTestVideoRecorder/BDSubWiz only ship with Visual Studio/Bitdefender, so a copy running from a staging folder is a strong side-load indicator. Rationale: Uses the three exact side-load host binaries named by Kaspersky/THN (BDSubWiz.exe, VSTestVideoRecorder.exe, GoogleDesktop.exe) plus their real vendor install paths as an allowlist so only relocated/staged copies alert. Cross-checked Securelist and THN. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://gbhackers.com/toddycat-uses-shadow-token/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1022/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/002/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running VSTestVideoRecorder.exe from a non-default portable Visual Studio / build-agent working directory
  • Bitdefender ConnectAgent installed to a custom drive letter outside a path literally containing 'Bitdefender'
  • Legacy Google Desktop reinstalled by a nostalgic user into a custom folder
  • Software-packaging/SCCM staging that copies vendor binaries to a temp deploy folder before install
  • Security-testing/red-team labs replicating the side-load for validation
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","ccmexec.exe","tiworker.exe","devenv.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full FolderPath, SHA256 and command line of the flagged binary; check whether a same-directory DLL (non-Microsoft/vendor signature, .NET+ConfuserEx) was loaded via DeviceImageLoadEvents on the same PID. 2) Contain: isolate the host and kill the process tree; block the offending DLL hash org-wide; look for the parent scheduled task and disable it. 3) Hunt: search all endpoints for the same SHA256/DLL, for the 'KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp' scheduled task, and for subsequent headless-browser/BackupFiles activity indicating STRD progressed to credential access.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where not(
      (FileName =~ "GoogleDesktop.exe" and FolderPath has @"\Google\Google Desktop Search\")
   or (FileName =~ "BDSubWiz.exe" and FolderPath has "Bitdefender")
   or (FileName =~ "VSTestVideoRecorder.exe" and (FolderPath has @"\Microsoft Visual Studio\" or FolderPath has @"\Common7\IDE\"))
  )
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\BDSubWiz.exe","\\VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","\\GoogleDesktop.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where not(
      (NewProcessName has "GoogleDesktop.exe" and NewProcessName has "\\Google\\Google Desktop Search\\")
   or (NewProcessName has "BDSubWiz.exe" and NewProcessName has "Bitdefender")
   or (NewProcessName has "VSTestVideoRecorder.exe" and (NewProcessName has "\\Microsoft Visual Studio\\" or NewProcessName has "\\Common7\\IDE\\"))
  )
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

Scheduled task impersonating Kaspersky EDR (KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp) to launch signed side-load host AIInstallation High
Hunts creation or invocation of a scheduled task whose name masquerades as Kaspersky's EDR agent ('KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp') — the exact persistence/masquerade ToddyCat used to launch the digitally signed Umbrij side-load binary. The string is unique to this campaign and does not correspond to any genuine Kaspersky task name. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim masquerade task name 'KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp' reported by Kaspersky — a fabricated name (genuine Kaspersky runs avp.exe / 'Kaspersky Endpoint Security'), so any hit is high-fidelity. Cross-checked Securelist and THN. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/toddycat-linked-umbrij-malware-abuses.html
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal detection-engineering or purple-team replaying this named IOC in a lab
  • Custom EDR-deployment automation a SOC named after Kaspersky (rare, and would not use this exact spelling)
  • A saved hunting query/ticket text echoing the task name into a shell that then logs it
  • SIEM validation harness generating synthetic events with the IOC string
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "purpleteam" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "atomic-red-team"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the task target binary via the command line / 4698 XML — expect a signed BDSubWiz/VSTestVideoRecorder/GoogleDesktop path; verify no genuine Kaspersky product justifies it. 2) Contain: delete the scheduled task (schtasks /delete), isolate the host, and capture the referenced binary + adjacent DLL for analysis. 3) Hunt: pivot to the task's action binary across the fleet, review DeviceImageLoadEvents for the ConfuserEx DLL, and check for downstream headless-browser BackupFiles activity.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

Chromium headless remote-debugging launch against copied BackupFiles profile (STRD OAuth token theft) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the core Shadow-Token-via-Remote-Debug step: chrome.exe/msedge.exe launched with a remote-debugging port and/or headless flag using a user-data-dir under a 'BackupFiles' folder (the profile Umbrij copies). This gives Puppeteer control over an already-authenticated Gmail session to mint an OAuth authorization code. Rationale: Combines the article's exact tradecraft — headless Chromium + remote debugging port + the copied 'BackupFiles' user profile — into one command-line shape unique to STRD; the BackupFiles token removes almost all legitimate remote-debugging noise. Cross-checked Securelist and THN. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://gbhackers.com/toddycat-uses-shadow-token/
ATT&CKT1185 T1539 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Front-end developer/QA automation launching headless Chrome with --remote-debugging-port (but with a project profile dir, not 'BackupFiles')
  • Puppeteer/Playwright CI runners on a build box
  • Selenium browser-grid nodes
  • Browser-based synthetic monitoring agents
  • Security testing replicating the STRD chain in a lab
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node.exe","code.exe","devenv.exe","cypress.exe","playwright.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the --user-data-dir and --remote-debugging-port values; confirm the profile path resolves under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Google\Chrome\BackupFiles or \Microsoft\Edge\BackupFiles and identify the parent process (likely the side-load host). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the browser + parent tree, and — critically — force-revoke Google OAuth grants for the affected user at myaccount.google.com/connections, specifically 'Google Workspace Migration for Microsoft Outlook' / 'Google Workspace Sync for Microsoft Outlook'. 3) Hunt: review Google Workspace API/audit logs for token exchange and Gmail/Drive/Contacts access from unfamiliar clients, and check for exfil of Umbrij's log file containing the auth code.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "BackupFiles"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port","--headless")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\chrome.exe","\\msedge.exe")
| where CommandLine has "BackupFiles"
| where CommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port" or CommandLine has "--headless"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: Chromium Headless Remote-Debugging Launch Against BackupFiles Profile (ToddyCat STRD)

status: experimental

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Umbrij copies Chrome/Edge credential stores into %LOCALAPPDATA%\...\BackupFiles AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the collection step where Umbrij duplicates each browser profile's secret stores (Login Data, Web Data, Secure Preferences, Local State, cookies) into a 'BackupFiles' directory under the Chrome/Edge LocalAppData folder so it can relaunch headless with active session cookies. File writes of these named stores into a BackupFiles path are not produced by normal browser operation. Rationale: Uses the exact directory ('BackupFiles') and the verbatim list of browser secret files Umbrij copies, scoped to the Chrome/Edge LocalAppData roots named in the article — a file-write shape browsers never produce themselves. Cross-checked Securelist and THN. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/toddycat-linked-umbrij-malware-abuses.html
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup/migration utilities that snapshot browser profiles into a folder a user happened to name 'BackupFiles'
  • IT profile-migration tooling copying Login Data during PC refresh
  • Forensic/DFIR collection scripts staging browser artifacts
  • Enterprise browser-sync agents duplicating profile data
  • Red-team validation of the Umbrij chain
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","explorer.exe","robocopy.exe","usmt.exe","scanstate.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the writing process (ContextImageFileName / InitiatingProcessFileName) — expect a signed side-load host, not the browser itself; confirm the target files include Login Data/Web Data/Local State. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the writer and any headless browser it spawned, and revoke the user's Google OAuth grants (myaccount.google.com/connections) plus reset Google session cookies. 3) Hunt: search for a subsequent headless remote-debugging launch against the BackupFiles profile, exfil of Umbrij's verbose log (which stores the auth code), and Google Workspace API access from unrecognised clients.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has "BackupFiles"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Login Data For Account","Web Data","Cookies","Secure Preferences","Preferences","Local State")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "BackupFiles"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Login Data For Account","Web Data","Cookies","Secure Preferences","Preferences","Local State")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent

    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents

SecurityEvent

        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66") or SHA1 in~ ("1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66") or MD5 in~ ("1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66") or SHA1 in~ ("1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66") or MD5 in~ ("1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Inbound exploitation of Cisco Unified CM WebDialer SSRF (CVE-2026-20230) from campaign infra · [LLM] Cisco Unified CM SSRF file:// arbitrary file-write payload (CVE-2026-20230)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Rogue Apache Axis AdminService / JSP webshell on Cisco Unified CM (CVE-2026-20230 post-exploit)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Inbound exploitation of Cisco Unified CM WebDialer SSRF (CVE-2026-20230) from campaign infra AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to the Cisco Unified CM WebDialer service that carry SSRF exploit markers (file://, Apache Axis AdminService) or originate from the Defused-reported campaign IP 156.146.38.167. This is the initial-access step Cisco confirmed is under active exploitation. Rationale: Anchored on the corroborated exploit chain (WebDialer service + Apache Axis AdminService + file:// SSRF) confirmed by Cisco's advisory, SOCRadar and DarkReading; the campaign IP 156.146.38.167 is currently single-source (Defused) so it is used as a booster, not the sole anchor. Defender/Falcon left empty because CUCM is a Linux Tomcat appliance not onboarded to EDR — detection lives on the wire (CEF) and in appliance syslog. Cross-checked against: • https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-cucm-ssrf-cXPnHcW • https://socradar.io/blog/cve-2026-20230-cisco-unified-cm-webdialer-ssrf/ • https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/less-than-24-hours-attackers-weaponize-cisco-cucm-flaw
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WebDialer click-to-call SOAP traffic from internal CTI/UC applications (will lack file:// and AdminService markers)
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Tenable/Qualys/Rapid7) probing the WebDialer endpoint from a known scan subnet
  • Internal penetration-test or Cisco TAC-guided validation of the patch from a corporate source IP
  • Security-team replaying the public PoC from a sanctioned research host
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestURL has "webdialer" and not (RequestURL has_any ("file://","file:/","AdminService","/axis/")) and SourceIP !in (CampaignIPs))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the destination is a Unified CM host and inspect the full RequestURL for a file:// scheme or Axis AdminService call; check whether WebDialer is enabled and whether the CUCM version predates 14SU6/15SU5. 2) Contain: block SourceIP 156.146.38.167 at the perimeter, disable the WebDialer service (Cisco's interim mitigation), and restrict WebDialer to trusted management networks. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same DestinationIP for follow-on /axis/ AdminService requests and newly created .jsp files under the Tomcat web root (see webshell UC), and review CUCM install/security logs for unexpected files.
let CampaignIPs = dynamic(["156.146.38.167"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where RequestURL has "webdialer"
| where SourceIP in (CampaignIPs)
   or RequestURL has_any ("file://", "file:/", "AdminService", "/axis/", "%2Ffile", "%66%69%6c%65")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction, RequestClientApplication
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
title: Cisco Unified CM WebDialer SSRF Exploitation Inbound (CVE-2026-20230)

description: Inbound HTTP request to the Cisco Unified CM WebDialer service carrying SSRF exploit markers or from the reported campaign IP for CVE-2026-20230.

Cisco Unified CM SSRF file:// arbitrary file-write payload (CVE-2026-20230) AIExploitation High
Hunts HTTP requests to a Unified CM host whose URI/query embeds a file:// scheme, the mechanism Defused observed attackers using to write attacker-controlled files onto the appliance via the WebDialer SSRF. Content-pivot detection independent of source IP. Rationale: Uses the article's specific technique string 'properly constructed file:// payloads to create files' plus the corroborated Axis/WebDialer target paths; matches on request content so it fires regardless of rotating source IPs. URL-encoded variants included because SSRF payloads are commonly percent-encoded to bypass filters. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/cve-2026-20230-cisco-unified-cm-webdialer-ssrf/ • https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-cucm-ssrf-cXPnHcW
ATT&CKT1190 T1105
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners injecting file:// test strings during authorized SSRF assessments
  • WAF/IPS logging the raw payload of a blocked request (verify DeviceAction shows block, not allow)
  • Developers or Cisco TAC reproducing the PoC in a lab that shares the SIEM
  • Legitimate application passing a file: parameter unrelated to CUCM (excluded by the webdialer/axis/ccmadmin path requirement)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceAction !in~ ("blocked","denied","drop","reset")
Response runbook
1) Triage: decode the file:// path in RequestURL to see what the attacker attempted to read/write, and confirm whether the WAF allowed or blocked (DeviceAction). 2) Contain: if allowed, isolate the CUCM host from untrusted networks, disable WebDialer, and snapshot the appliance for forensics before patching to 14SU6/15SU5. 3) Hunt: search the same host for follow-on /axis/services/AdminService calls and newly written .jsp files, and review CUCM audit logs for unexpected OS-level files created around the request timestamp.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where RequestURL has_any ("webdialer", "/axis/", "/ccmadmin/")
| where RequestURL has_any ("file://", "file:%2F%2F", "file:/", "%66%69%6c%65%3a")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Rogue Apache Axis AdminService / JSP webshell on Cisco Unified CM (CVE-2026-20230 post-exploit) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the post-SSRF stage where attackers invoke the Apache Axis AdminService on the CUCM Tomcat stack to deploy a rogue SOAP service and then access an attacker-dropped .jsp webshell in the web root — the code-execution/persistence tail of the CVE-2026-20230 chain. Rationale: Targets the corroborated post-exploit chain (SOCRadar/DarkReading: rogue Apache Axis service deployed via AdminService, then a JSP file-writer/command shell in the Tomcat web dir). AdminService invocation and new .jsp access on a production CUCM are highly abnormal, giving a sharp signal distinct from the initial SSRF request. Cross-checked against: • https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/less-than-24-hours-attackers-weaponize-cisco-cucm-flaw • https://socradar.io/blog/cve-2026-20230-cisco-unified-cm-webdialer-ssrf/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cisco built-in .jsp application pages accessed during normal CCMAdmin/Self-Care usage (baseline the specific known .jsp set)
  • Cisco upgrade/COP file installation touching Tomcat webapps
  • Authorized admin using legitimate Axis-based CUCM management functions from a management host
  • Vulnerability scanner fingerprinting the /axis/ path
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestURL contains ".jsp" and DestinationHostName !has "cucm" and RequestURL !has "AdminService")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the exact .jsp path and whether it exists in a stock CUCM image; a non-catalog .jsp or any external-sourced GET/POST to /axis/services/AdminService is high-confidence malicious. 2) Contain: isolate the CUCM host, capture the .jsp and Tomcat logs, and treat the appliance as root-compromised — plan rebuild/restore rather than in-place cleanup. 3) Hunt: correlate back to the originating SSRF file:// request and source IP, review outbound connections from the CUCM host for C2/reverse shell, and check for credential/config exfiltration and lateral movement from the appliance.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where RequestURL has_any ("/axis/services/AdminService", "AdminService", "/axis/services")
   or (RequestURL contains ".jsp" and RequestURL has_any ("/webdialer/", "/axis/", "/ccmadmin/", "/cucm-uds/"))
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,

// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010

SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] SharePoint IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawns shell/LOLBIN — CVE-2026-45659 deserialization RCE
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SharePoint worker (w3wp.exe) writes .aspx web shell into LAYOUTS web root — CVE-2026-45659 post-exploit
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

SharePoint IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawns shell/LOLBIN — CVE-2026-45659 deserialization RCE AIExploitation High
Hunts the code-execution step of the CVE-2026-45659 SharePoint deserialization RCE: the gadget chain runs in the context of the SharePoint application-pool worker (w3wp.exe), which then spawns a command interpreter or LOLBIN. A production SharePoint server's IIS worker process essentially never spawns cmd/powershell/certutil, so this is high-fidelity for exploitation. Rationale: Grounded in the article's core claim that CVE-2026-45659 lets an authenticated attacker 'execute code remotely on the SharePoint Server' via deserialization; corroborating write-ups (Akamai, Trellix, Rapid7) confirm the payload runs as the w3wp.exe app-pool identity, and w3wp spawning cmd/powershell is the canonical exploitation signal for SharePoint deserialization RCE. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/microsoft-patches-sharepoint-rce-flaw.html • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/05/26/sharepoint-vulnerability-cve-2026-45659/ • https://www.akamai.com/blog/security-research/sharepoint-vulnerability-rce-active-exploitation-detections-mitigations • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/toolshell-unleashed-decoding-the-sharepoint-attack-chain/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-zero-day-exploitation-of-microsoft-sharepoint-servers-cve-2025-53770/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SharePoint timer/health scripts or admin PSConfig runs that spawn cmd/powershell under the STS/app-pool context during patching
  • Monitoring agents (SCOM, custom probes) invoking net.exe or whoami.exe under the IIS worker for health checks
  • Backup or DLP integrations that shell out from a custom SharePoint web part
  • Non-SharePoint IIS sites sharing a w3wp.exe binary name where a web app legitimately shells out
  • Post-patch validation tooling that queries app-pool identity via whoami
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("psconfig", "Microsoft.SharePoint.Administration") and InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the host is a SharePoint server and pull the full child command line + SHA256; look for encoded/download strings, machine-key/web.config reads, or recon (whoami/net). Check whether the CVE-2026-45659 May 2026 update (SharePoint 2016/2019/Subscription Edition) is installed. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the server from the network, kill the offending process tree, and preserve w3wp memory/IIS logs; if compromise confirmed, rotate the SharePoint MachineKey/ASP.NET keys (stolen keys enable forged-request persistence). 3) HUNT: Pivot to UC2 (web-shell writes into LAYOUTS), review IIS logs for the originating authenticated account and source IP, and sweep other internet-exposed SharePoint servers for the same w3wp child-spawn pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\regsvr32.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\curl.exe","\\net.exe","\\net1.exe","\\whoami.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SharePoint worker (w3wp.exe) writes .aspx web shell into LAYOUTS web root — CVE-2026-45659 post-exploit AIInstallation High
Hunts the persistence step after CVE-2026-45659 exploitation: the SharePoint IIS worker process writing a new web-accessible handler (.aspx/.ashx/.asmx) into the SharePoint LAYOUTS/Web Server Extensions directory. Legitimate SharePoint provisions these files via the installer/solution deployment, not from the live w3wp worker at runtime — so a runtime write here is a strong web-shell indicator. Rationale: The article states CVE-2026-45659 grants RCE with the SharePoint process's permissions; corroborating SharePoint-RCE research (Akamai, Trellix, Rapid7) shows attackers immediately drop .aspx web shells into the LAYOUTS web root (C:\Program Files\Common Files\Microsoft Shared\Web Server Extensions\..\TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS\), and a runtime write of a new handler by w3wp.exe is not legitimate SharePoint behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://www.akamai.com/blog/security-research/sharepoint-vulnerability-rce-active-exploitation-detections-mitigations • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/toolshell-unleashed-decoding-the-sharepoint-attack-chain/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-zero-day-exploitation-of-microsoft-sharepoint-servers-cve-2025-53770/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/microsoft-patches-sharepoint-rce-flaw.html
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint cumulative-update / PSConfig deployment writing provisioned .aspx pages into LAYOUTS during patching windows
  • WSP solution package deployment (Add-SPSolution/Install-SPSolution) staging application pages
  • Third-party SharePoint add-ins provisioning custom application pages at first activation
  • Admin manual copy of a legitimate application page authored under the app-pool account
  • Antivirus/DLP quarantine-restore operations rewriting an existing .aspx in place
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("psconfig", "Install-SPSolution", "Add-SPSolution", "stsadm"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Retrieve and read the written file — a short/obfuscated page with eval/Request/Process.Start or MachineKey/web.config access is a web shell; note file SHA256, path, and timestamp, and confirm the May 2026 CVE-2026-45659 patch state. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the server, quarantine/remove the file (retain a copy), kill any live w3wp child process tree, and rotate SharePoint MachineKey/ASP.NET machine keys since forged-request persistence survives file removal. 3) HUNT: Correlate to UC1 (w3wp spawning shells), search IIS logs for POST requests immediately preceding the file write to identify the authenticated account and source IP, and sweep all SharePoint servers for other recently written handlers in LAYOUTS.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FolderPath has @"\TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS\" or FolderPath has @"\Web Server Extensions\"
| where FileName endswith ".aspx" or FileName endswith ".ashx" or FileName endswith ".asmx"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where ActingProcessName endswith "w3wp.exe"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS\" or TargetFilePath has @"\Web Server Extensions\"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".aspx" or TargetFileName endswith ".ashx" or TargetFileName endswith ".asmx"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45659")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)

| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"

SecurityEvent

| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Langflow CVE-2025-3248 unauthenticated RCE via /api/v1/validate/code · [LLM] Langflow/Python web-service process spawning shell or downloader child · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Cron persistence written by web-service process (JADEPUFFER 30-min beacon) · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] JADEPUFFER C2/staging beacon to 45.131.66.106 and 64.20.53.230 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] JADEPUFFER database ransom note / mass-destruction indicators (README_RANSOM) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Langflow CVE-2025-3248 unauthenticated RCE via /api/v1/validate/code AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP POST requests to Langflow's code-validation endpoint, the vector JADEPUFFER abused (CVE-2025-3248) to run arbitrary Python with no authentication. Article-specific because it pins the exact vulnerable Langflow endpoint rather than generic web exploitation. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE-2025-3248 exploit endpoint (/api/v1/validate/code) named in the article as the Langflow way-in; POST to this path from external clients is the observable footprint of the RCE.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Langflow developers validating code components through the UI
  • Internal CI/CD pipelines building or testing flows against the Langflow API
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys) probing the endpoint
  • Langflow health-check or monitoring tooling hitting /api/v1 paths
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the Langflow version — if < 1.3.0 the host is exploitable; check the source IP against threat intel and whether it is external/unauthenticated. 2) Contain: take the Langflow instance off the public internet (firewall/ACL) and rotate any API keys or cloud credentials stored in its environment. 3) Hunt: pivot to the host's DeviceProcessEvents for python spawning shells (UC2) and outbound beacons to 45.131.66.106 (UC3) within minutes of the POST.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod == "POST"
| where Url has "/api/v1/validate/code"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, UserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow/Python web-service process spawning shell or downloader child AIExploitation Medium
Detects the Langflow Python interpreter (or uvicorn/gunicorn) spawning a shell, curl/wget, or netcat child — the execution context created when CVE-2025-3248 code injection lands. Article-specific: Langflow runs Python and the agent 'mapped the machine, then swept it for secrets' via such child processes. Rationale: The article states Langflow runs Python and the agent used the RCE to 'map the machine and sweep for secrets' — that means the Langflow Python process spawning shells/downloaders, a high-signal parent→child pivot tying execution to the web service identity.
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1059.004 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow flows that legitimately shell out to run tools or install packages
  • Container entrypoint scripts where gunicorn/uvicorn forks helper shells at startup
  • Admin-authored Langflow custom components invoking curl/wget for data fetch
  • Health-check scripts run under the web service user
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("apt-get","pip install","pip3 install","yum install"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the child command line — reverse shells, curl to raw IPs, or env-var/credential grep (env, ~/.aws, ~/.config) are true positives; package installs are usually benign. 2) Contain: kill the process tree, isolate the host, and rotate every secret reachable from the Langflow environment (OpenAI/Anthropic/DeepSeek/Gemini keys, AWS/Azure/GCP/Alibaba/Tencent creds). 3) Hunt: check for the 30-minute cron beacon (UC4) and connections to 45.131.66.106 (UC3) from the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn","langflow") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "langflow"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn","langflow")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

JADEPUFFER C2/staging beacon to 45.131.66.106 and 64.20.53.230 AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any outbound connection to JADEPUFFER's C2 (45.131.66.106, beacon to :4444/beacon) or claimed staging server (64.20.53.230). Pure IOC match against the addresses Sysdig published for this operation. Rationale: Directly matches Sysdig's published indicators: C2 45.131.66.106 (beacon to :4444/beacon every 30 min) and staging 64.20.53.230 — fixed IPs give a near-zero-FP alerting signal.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel platform or sandbox detonating samples that reach the same IPs
  • Security researchers scanning the C2 infrastructure from corporate ranges
  • Shared-hosting IP reuse after the C2 is taken down and the address is re-leased
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal host and the process making the connection (InitiatingProcessFileName / ContextImageFileName) — a web-service or cron-invoked curl is a strong true positive. 2) Contain: block both IPs at the egress firewall, isolate the host, and preserve memory before reimaging. 3) Hunt: search all hosts for the 30-minute beaconing cadence to :4444/beacon and for the cron persistence entry (UC4) that drives it.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("45.131.66.106","64.20.53.230") or (RemoteUrl has "45.131.66.106" and RemoteUrl has "/beacon")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("45.131.66.106","64.20.53.230")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
title: JADEPUFFER C2/Staging IP Beacon

Cron persistence written by web-service process (JADEPUFFER 30-min beacon) AIInstallation Medium
Detects a Langflow/Python or shell process writing to cron paths (/etc/cron*, /var/spool/cron, /etc/crontab) — the mechanism JADEPUFFER used to add a scheduled task pinging its server every 30 minutes. Article-specific: the persistence is a scheduled task installed by the compromised web service. Rationale: Article states the agent 'set up a way back in, adding a scheduled task that pinged the attacker's server every 30 minutes' — on Linux that is a cron write, and a cron write authored by the web-service process is highly abnormal.
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Configuration management (Ansible/Puppet/Chef) deploying cron jobs
  • Application installers or package post-install scripts adding cron entries
  • Admin editing crontab via an interactive shell during maintenance
  • Backup/monitoring agents registering their own scheduled jobs
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ansible","puppet","chef-client","salt-minion"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the cron entry — an entry invoking curl/wget to a raw IP (especially 45.131.66.106) on a 30-minute schedule is a confirmed true positive. 2) Contain: remove the cron entry, isolate the host, and block the beacon IP. 3) Hunt: correlate to the C2 beacon (UC3) and the initial Langflow RCE (UC1) on the same host, and check for the README_RANSOM impact stage (UC5).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/etc/cron","/var/spool/cron","/etc/crontab")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn","langflow","sh","bash","dash")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/cron","/var/spool/cron","/etc/crontab")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn","langflow","bash","sh","dash")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

JADEPUFFER database ransom note / mass-destruction indicators (README_RANSOM) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects execution containing JADEPUFFER's unique ransom artefacts — the README_RANSOM table name, the Bitcoin address 3J98t1WpEZ73CNmQviecrnyiWrnqRhWNLy, or the Proton contact e78393397@proton.me — the impact stage that encrypted 1,342 Nacos configs and dropped/deleted databases. Rationale: README_RANSOM (the ransom table name), the Bitcoin address, and the Proton contact are unique published IOCs from this operation; any process command line carrying them is unambiguous impact-stage activity.
ATT&CKT1486 T1485 T1565.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Incident responders or threat hunters grepping for these IOC strings during investigation
  • Detection-rule deployment or SIEM content that echoes the IOC strings into command lines
  • Backup/restore tooling referencing a recovered README_RANSOM table during remediation
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host and whether the command actually created a README_RANSOM table or issued DROP/DELETE against MySQL/Nacos — the article notes the key is never saved, so treat data as unrecoverable. 2) Contain: isolate the database/Nacos host immediately, snapshot for forensics, and revoke the root DB credentials and the planted Nacos admin account. 3) Hunt: trace back to the Langflow RCE (UC1), the C2 beacon (UC3), and check MinIO for the minioadmin:minioadmin default-login access and any secret-sweeping activity.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("README_RANSOM","3J98t1WpEZ73CNmQviecrnyiWrnqRhWNLy","e78393397@proton.me")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("README_RANSOM","3J98t1WpEZ73CNmQviecrnyiWrnqRhWNLy","e78393397@proton.me")
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("README_RANSOM","3J98t1WpEZ73CNmQviecrnyiWrnqRhWNLy","e78393397@proton.me")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.

   or Url has_any (BadDomains)

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-3248", "CVE-2021-29441")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-3248", "CVE-2021-29441")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2025-3248", "CVE-2021-29441")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2025-3248", "CVE-2021-29441")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,

// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs

| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),

         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
