FortiBleed 'adminin' backdoor local account creation and logon AIInstallation High
Hunts creation and subsequent use of a local account named 'adminin' — the exact backdoor username SOCRadar found planted on FortiBleed-compromised systems for persistent access. Fires on both the account-creation command and any logon by that account. Rationale: Anchored on the exact backdoor username 'adminin' from the article's code block; SOCRadar/SecurityWeek independently confirm the operators 'make backdoor users' on compromised FortiBleed hosts, making this a near-zero-FP named-account detection. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/fortibleed-fortinet-firewalls-compromised/ • https://www.securityweek.com/fortibleed-86000-fortinet-device-credentials-compromised/ • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/active-fortibleed-campaign-impacting-fortinet-devices-across-194-countries/
ATT&CKT1136.001 T1078.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An organization legitimately standardizes admin service accounts on a similar naming scheme (e.g. 'adminintl' truncated in a script)
  • Red-team / purple-team exercise recreating the FortiBleed backdoor for detection validation
  • IT provisioning template that reuses a generic bootstrap account name
  • Migration tooling that recreates local accounts during OS re-imaging
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full DeviceProcessEvents/4720 record — who (InitiatingProcessAccountName) created 'adminin', from what parent process, and whether it was added to Administrators/Remote Desktop groups. Correlate the logon RemoteIP against known-good admin subnets. 2) Contain: disable/delete the 'adminin' account, force-reset any admin credentials on the host, and isolate the device from the network if it is an internet-facing appliance mgmt host. 3) Hunt: sweep every host and FortiGate for the same account name, look for outbound connections to unfamiliar hosting IPs, and check for downloaded FortiGate config files and the FortigateSniffer tool.
union
 (DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has "adminin"
  | where (FileName in~ ("net.exe","net1.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "user" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/add","-add"))
       or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("New-LocalUser","Add-LocalGroupMember"))
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal="LocalAccountCreated", Account="adminin", Detail=ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName),
 (DeviceLogonEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where AccountName =~ "adminin"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal="BackdoorAccountLogon", Account=AccountName, Detail=strcat("LogonType=", tostring(LogonType), " RemoteIP=", RemoteIP), InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName=AccountDomain)
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (EventID in (4720,4732,4728,4726) and TargetUserName =~ "adminin")
     or (EventID == 4624 and TargetUserName =~ "adminin")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventID, Activity, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName, IpAddress, LogonType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: FortiBleed 'adminin' Backdoor Local Account Creation

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/\bnet1?\s+user\s+adminin\b.*(\/add|-add)/i

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("net.exe","net1.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")) Processes.process="*adminin*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process,"(?i)(user\s+adminin.*(/add|-add)|New-LocalUser.*adminin|Add-LocalGroupMember.*adminin)") | sort - lastTime
Credential-stuffing burst culminating in success against FortiGate SSL-VPN / SSO AIExploitation Medium
Detects the FortiBleed reuse pattern: many failed authentications from a single source IP across multiple usernames followed by at least one success — the harvested/cracked Fortinet credentials being stuffed against SSL-VPN gateways and reused against Entra SSO. Rationale: The article and multiple corroborating sources state credential stuffing is the PRIMARY collection/reuse mechanism of FortiBleed; the one-IP/many-users/many-fails-then-success shape against FortiGate SSL-VPN and Entra SSO is the article-specific signature of stolen-credential reuse, not a generic brute-force template. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/what-is-fortibleed/ • https://www.securityweek.com/fortibleed-86000-fortinet-device-credentials-compromised/ • https://www.bitsight.com/blog/security-alert-fortibleed-fortinet-vpn-credentials-firewall-exposed
ATT&CKT1110.004 T1110.003 T1078
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Corporate NAT/VPN concentrator egressing many users behind one public IP triggering the distinct-user threshold
  • Misconfigured mobile client or expired-password loop generating repeated failures then a success after reset
  • Security scanner / authenticated vulnerability scan hitting the VPN portal
  • SSO migration event causing bulk re-authentication from a proxy IP
Suppression filter
// exclude known corporate egress / NAT gateways before alerting:
| where SourceIP !in ("") // populate with your published corporate egress IPs; keep external-only IPs in scope
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is external and not a corporate NAT gateway; enumerate which usernames succeeded and whether MFA was satisfied. 2) Contain: force password reset + session revocation on every successfully-authenticated account from that IP, block the source IP at the FortiGate and IdP, and enforce MFA on SSL-VPN if absent. 3) Hunt: check whether any of the compromised accounts have Fortinet-managed credentials matching the FortiBleed dumps, review those accounts for 'adminin' creation, config downloads, and lateral movement toward file servers/backup hosts.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| summarize Failures = countif(ErrorCode != 0), Successes = countif(ErrorCode == 0), DistinctUsers = dcount(AccountUpn), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), SampleApps = make_set(Application, 5) by IPAddress
| where DistinctUsers >= 10 and Failures >= 20 and Successes >= 1   // one IP, 10+ users, 20+ fails, >=1 success = stuffing signature
| order by Failures desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Activity has_any ("ssl-login","sslvpn","vpn","login") or Message has_any ("SSL VPN","login")
| extend Outcome = tolower(coalesce(EventOutcome, DeviceAction, Message))
| summarize Failures = countif(Outcome has_any ("fail","deny","error")), Successes = countif(Outcome has_any ("success","accept","ok","tunnel-up")), DistinctUsers = dcount(DestinationHostName), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP
| where DistinctUsers >= 10 and Failures >= 20 and Successes >= 1
| order by Failures desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.status.errorCode:50126
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where (Authentication.app="fortigate" OR Authentication.app="*ssl*vpn*" OR Authentication.app="*vpn*") by Authentication.src Authentication.action Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | stats sum(eval(if(action="failure",count,0))) as failures sum(eval(if(action="success",count,0))) as successes dc(user) as user_count values(user) as users by src | where failures >= 20 AND successes >= 1 AND user_count >= 10 | sort - failures
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where (Authentication.app="fortigate" OR Authentication.app="*ssl*vpn*" OR Authentication.app="*vpn*") by Authentication.src Authentication.action Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | stats sum(eval(if(action="failure",count,0))) as failures sum(eval(if(action="success",count,0))) as successes dc(user) as user_count values(user) as users by src | where failures >= 20 AND successes >= 1 AND user_count >= 10 | sort - failures
FortiGate admin login and configuration download from external IP AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the FortiBleed initial-access footprint on edge devices: administrative authentication to a FortiGate from a public/Internet source IP paired with configuration backup/download activity — the exact behaviour that produced the exposed cache of FortiGate config files. Rationale: Anchored on the article's 'downloaded FortiGate configuration files' collection artifact plus the mass edge-device compromise; scoping FortiGate config-download/admin-login to a non-private (external) source IP flags attacker administrative access rather than internal management. Defender/Falcon/Datadog left empty as FortiGate appliance logs do not ship to those platforms. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/fortibleed-fortinet-firewalls-compromised/ • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4186790/fortibleed-campaign-exposes-75000-fortinet-firewalls-worldwide.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1602.002 T1078
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate remote administrator managing the FortiGate over the public interface from a home/ISP IP
  • MSP/outsourced NOC performing scheduled configuration backups from their own cloud IP
  • Vendor support session downloading config for troubleshooting
  • Monitoring tool pulling config snapshots via API from an external SaaS source
Suppression filter
| where SrcIP !in ("") // populate with approved external management source IPs (MSP/NOC/admin home IPs)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the admin account and source IP; verify against the approved management-IP allowlist and change-management tickets for a config backup at that time. 2) Contain: if unrecognized, disable/rotate the admin credential, restrict the mgmt interface to trusted IPs / VPN only, and pull the current config to diff against baseline for rogue admins ('adminin'), added VPN users, or a packet-sniffer/FortigateSniffer artifact. 3) Hunt: review VPN auth logs for stuffing bursts, check for outbound connections to unfamiliar hosting IPs, and correlate the org against INC/Lynx leak-site listings.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Message has_any ("Configuration is downloaded","config backup","backup config","Admin login successful","login successful") or Activity has_any ("download","backup","admin-login")
| extend SrcIP = SourceIP
| where isnotempty(SrcIP) and not(ipv4_is_private(SrcIP))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName = DeviceExternalID, SrcIP, DestinationHostName, SourceUserName, Activity, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.app="fortigate" Authentication.action="success" (Authentication.user="admin" OR Authentication.user="*admin*") by Authentication.src Authentication.dest Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where NOT (cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8",src) OR cidrmatch("172.16.0.0/12",src) OR cidrmatch("192.168.0.0/16",src)) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.app="fortigate" Authentication.action="success" (Authentication.user="admin" OR Authentication.user="*admin*") by Authentication.src Authentication.dest Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where NOT (cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8",src) OR cidrmatch("172.16.0.0/12",src) OR cidrmatch("192.168.0.0/16",src)) | sort - lastTime
Outbound connection to FortiBleed operator infrastructure 85.11.187.8 AICommand & Control Low
Watches for any host or edge device communicating with 85.11.187.8, the FortiBleed operator server IP surfaced in the article. Single-source IOC — ship as hunting/enrichment, validate before alerting. Rationale: Uses the single pre-extracted network IOC (85.11.187.8) from the article. It could NOT be corroborated by a second source (ThreatFox/OTX/other vendor write-ups), so confidence is Low and it is scoped as hunting/enrichment — validate reputation before alerting.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The IP is shared hosting and later serves a benign tenant after takedown/reassignment
  • Threat-intel or ASM scanner in your environment probing the flagged IP
  • Security researcher/sandbox traffic to the IP from a lab host
  • Stale IOC firing on historical benign traffic if the address was previously legitimate
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm current reputation of 85.11.187.8 (VT/ThreatFox/passive DNS) and identify the initiating process/user and data volume (bytes out). 2) Contain: block the IP at perimeter/EDR, and if the source is a FortiGate or server staging harvested data, isolate it. 3) Hunt: expand to the wider operator fleet by pivoting on ASN/hosting neighbors, look for config/credential archive uploads, 'adminin' accounts, and any Lynx/INC follow-on activity on the same host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "85.11.187.8"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
 (CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DestinationIP == "85.11.187.8" or SourceIP == "85.11.187.8" | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, SentBytes, ReceivedBytes, SourceUserName),
 (ImNetworkSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DstIpAddr == "85.11.187.8" or SrcIpAddr == "85.11.187.8" | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkBytes)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Lynx/INC ransomware mass file encryption via .lynx extension AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the impact stage the FortiBleed access ultimately fed: bulk creation/rename of files with the '.lynx' extension by a single process, the hallmark of Lynx (INC rebrand) ransomware encryption. Corroborated extension across multiple vendor analyses. Rationale: The article explicitly links FortiBleed access to Lynx/INC ransomware impact; Unit42, Nextron, FortiGuard and Rapid7 independently confirm Lynx appends the unique '.lynx' extension and drops README.txt, so bulk '.lynx' writes by one process is a high-fidelity, article-specific impact detection. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/inc-ransomware-rebrand-to-lynx/ • https://www.nextron-systems.com/2024/10/11/in-depth-analysis-of-lynx-ransomware/ • https://www.fortinet.com/blog/threat-research/ransomware-roundup-lynx • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2024/09/12/ransomware-groups-demystified-lynx-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1486 T1490 T1657
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate application or dataset that coincidentally uses a '.lynx' file extension (rare; e.g. niche lynx browser cache/config artifacts)
  • Backup/restore of a previously-encrypted dataset re-introducing .lynx files
  • Security team detonating a Lynx sample in a sandbox on a monitored host
  • Renaming utility batch-appending '.lynx' during a controlled DFIR exercise
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and account, confirm whether README.txt ransom notes were dropped in the same directories and whether Volume Shadow Copies were deleted. 2) Contain: immediately isolate the host from the network, kill/suspend the encrypting process, and preserve memory and a disk image; check for spread to file servers/backup infrastructure (Veeam/MSSQL/Exchange). 3) Hunt: trace the intrusion back — FortiGate VPN stuffing logins, 'adminin' backdoor accounts, config downloads, and outbound staging to unfamiliar hosting IPs — and cross-reference the org against INC/Lynx leak-site listings; engage IR and preserve keys for possible decryption recovery.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName endswith ".lynx"
| summarize FileCount = dcount(FolderPath), SampleFiles = make_set(FileName, 5), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Proc = any(InitiatingProcessFileName), ProcCmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where FileCount >= 25   // 25 = mass-encryption burst; lower to 1 for max sensitivity given unique extension
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileExtension =~ "lynx" or TargetFileName endswith ".lynx"
| summarize FileCount = dcount(TargetFilePath), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Proc = any(ActingProcessName) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where FileCount >= 25
| order by FirstSeen desc

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-24858")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-24858")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-24858")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-24858")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity

DeviceFileEvents

| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

ImFileEvent

| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)

| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

            - '\svchost.exe'

falsepositives:

level: high

        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

New ChocoPoC malware targets researchers via trojanized PoC exploits

BleepingComputer
2026-07-01 7 use cases 3 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

Multiple weaponized proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits on GitHub were found delivering a Python-based remote access trojan (RAT) named ChocoPoC that can execute commands and steal sensitive data in a campaign believed to target cybersecurity researchers. [...]

CVEsCVE-2025-64446 CVE-2025-55182 CVE-2025-14847 CVE-2026-0257 CVE-2026-10520 CVE-2026-50751 CVE-2026-48908
ATT&CKT1190 T1204.002 T1555.003
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix
Phase 1
Reconnaissance
Detected
Phase 2
Weaponization
Detected
Phase 3
Delivery
Detected
Phase 4
Exploitation
Detected
Phase 5
Installation
Detected
Phase 6
Command & Control
Detected
Phase 7
Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Malicious ChocoPoC PyPI package install (frint/skytext/slogsec/logcrypt.cryptography) from cloned PoC repo
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Python loading native ChocoPoC extension (.so/.pyd) from skytext/frint package dir
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Python process contacting Mapbox dataset API (ChocoPoC download + exfil channel)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Python/shell reading browser credential & cookie stores (ChocoPoC stealer) · [LLM] Python bulk enumeration of sensitive files (.md/.txt/.db/.sqlite) from PoC context · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Malicious ChocoPoC PyPI package install (frint/skytext/slogsec/logcrypt.cryptography) from cloned PoC repo AIDelivery High
Hunts pip/python installing the named ChocoPoC supply-chain packages 'frint' and its transitive dependency 'skytext' (plus the older 'slogsec' and 'logcrypt.cryptography' variants) into site-packages. This is the delivery step where cloning a trojanized GitHub PoC auto-fetches the malicious dependency chain. Rationale: Uses the four exact PyPI package names Sekoia named (frint, skytext, slogsec, logcrypt.cryptography) written into site/dist-packages by pip/python — these strings do not appear in benign installs; corroborated via Sekoia research and a second BleepingComputer report. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sekoia.com/blog • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chocopoc-malware-delivered-via-trojanized-exploits-on-github/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate unrelated PyPI package genuinely named 'frint' if one is later published
  • Internal mirror/proxy re-caching these package names for takedown analysis
  • Malware-analysis lab intentionally detonating the sample
  • Security researcher reproducing the Sekoia findings in a sandbox
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--index-url https://pypi.org/simple") and FolderPath has "/analysis-sandbox/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent context — was pip invoked from a freshly cloned GitHub PoC directory (check InitiatingProcessParentFileName=git and the working dir)? Grab the SHA256 of any .so/.pyd under the skytext/frint dirs. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the python interpreter, and quarantine the site-packages/frint and /skytext directories; block outbound to api.mapbox.com from that host. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same package names org-wide, and check DeviceNetworkEvents for the host reaching Mapbox datasets (UC3) and browser-cred file access (UC4).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("pip","pip3","python","python3")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/frint/","/skytext/","/slogsec/","/logcrypt","\\frint\\","\\skytext\\","\\slogsec\\","\\logcrypt")
| where FolderPath has "site-packages" or FolderPath has "dist-packages"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("pip","pip3","python","python3")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/frint/","/skytext/","/slogsec/","/logcrypt","\\frint\\","\\skytext\\","\\slogsec\\","\\logcrypt")
| where TargetFilePath has "site-packages" or TargetFilePath has "dist-packages"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Python loading native ChocoPoC extension (.so/.pyd) from skytext/frint package dir AIInstallation High
Detects the Python interpreter loading a compiled native extension (.so/.pyd) directly from the malicious 'skytext' or 'frint' package directory. Per Sekoia this native extension auto-runs on PoC execution and decrypts embedded Python that stages the downloader — a distinct defense-evasion/unpacking step. Rationale: Anchors on the exact package dirs (skytext/frint) named by Sekoia AND the native-extension file type the article says auto-decrypts the next stage — python loading a .so from a PyPI package dir is normal, but from these named dirs it is the malicious unpacker. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sekoia.com/blog • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chocopoc-malware-delivered-via-trojanized-exploits-on-github/
ATT&CKT1027 T1140 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An unrelated legitimate future package named 'frint'/'skytext' shipping a native extension
  • Malware-analysis detonation in a sandbox
  • Researcher reproducing Sekoia's PoC
  • Package name collision on an internal PyPI mirror
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the loaded .so/.pyd and submit to sandbox/VT; confirm the module lives under site-packages/skytext or /frint and was loaded by an interpreter started from a cloned PoC dir. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the interpreter, quarantine the package dir, and snapshot memory if in-scope (decryption is in-process). 3) Hunt: search the host and org for outbound Mapbox dataset requests (UC3) and browser credential-store access (UC4) that follow this load.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/skytext/","/frint/","\\skytext\\","\\frint\\")
| where FileName endswith ".so" or FileName endswith ".pyd"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/skytext/","/frint/","\\skytext\\","\\frint\\")
| where FileName endswith ".so" or FileName endswith ".pyd"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Python process contacting Mapbox dataset API (ChocoPoC download + exfil channel) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects a Python interpreter making HTTP(S)/DNS requests to mapbox.com / api.mapbox.com. Sekoia reports ChocoPoC is retrieved FROM a Mapbox dataset and that Mapbox datasets are abused for data exfiltration — a python process (vs a mapping app or browser) reaching Mapbox is the C2/exfil tell. Rationale: Pairs the exact C2/exfil infrastructure Sekoia named (Mapbox datasets, mapbox.com) with the delivering process class (python) — Mapbox is legitimately called by browsers/mapping SDKs, so scoping to the python interpreter is what makes it a detection rather than noise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sekoia.com/blog • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chocopoc-malware-delivered-via-trojanized-exploits-on-github/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1567.002 T1102.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running a legitimate Python app that uses the Mapbox SDK/geocoding API
  • Data-science notebook (jupyter kernel = python) pulling map tiles
  • CI job testing a mapping integration
  • Internal GIS tooling written in Python
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("mapbox_sdk","geocoding","folium","mapboxgl") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "/opt/gis/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect InitiatingProcessCommandLine — is the python a known Mapbox-SDK app, or an interpreter launched from a cloned PoC/site-packages context? Pull the Mapbox dataset ID / URL path and request sizes. 2) Contain: block api.mapbox.com egress from the host, isolate if the python has no legitimate Mapbox use, and capture outbound payloads. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 (package install) and UC4 (browser cred theft) on the same host/user; check for a secondary HTTP server upload path used for larger files.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3")
| where RemoteUrl has "mapbox.com" or RemoteUrl has "api.mapbox.com"
| summarize Connections=count(), BytesContext=make_set(RemotePort,10), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by LastSeen desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "mapbox.com"
| summarize Queries=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery
| order by LastSeen desc

Python/shell reading browser credential & cookie stores (ChocoPoC stealer) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a Python interpreter or shell touching browser secret stores (Chrome/Edge 'Login Data'/'Cookies'/'Web Data', Firefox logins.json/key4.db/cookies.sqlite, macOS Keychains). ChocoPoC's stealer module collects browser passwords, cookies, autofill and history — scoping the reader to python/sh separates it from the browser itself. Rationale: Uses the exact stealer capability Sekoia listed (browser passwords/cookies/autofill/history) mapped to the concrete on-disk secret stores, gated to a python/shell reader so the browser's own access to those files is excluded. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sekoia.com/blog • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chocopoc-malware-delivered-via-trojanized-exploits-on-github/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539 T1555.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Browser-profile backup/sync scripts written in bash/python
  • Password-manager migration tooling exporting from Chrome/Firefox
  • IT scripted profile cleanup accessing cookie DBs
  • Developer automation using selenium/undetected-chromedriver that copies profile dirs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("backup","rsync","profile-sync-daemon","selenium","chromedriver")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating python/shell is not a sanctioned backup/sync tool — check its command line and parent, and whether it started from a cloned PoC dir. 2) Contain: isolate host, force-reset the user's saved-in-browser and SSO/session credentials (cookies imply session theft), revoke active tokens. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC3 (Mapbox exfil) for the same host/user, check shell-history and network-config file reads, and expand the browser-store read query across the fleet.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","bash","sh")
| where (FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","Web Data","cookies.sqlite","logins.json","key4.db","History"))
      or FolderPath has_any ("/.config/google-chrome/","/.mozilla/firefox/","/.config/BraveSoftware/","/.config/microsoft-edge/","/Library/Keychains/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","bash","sh")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/.config/google-chrome/","/.mozilla/firefox/","/.config/BraveSoftware/","/.config/microsoft-edge/","/Library/Keychains/","Login Data","cookies.sqlite","logins.json","key4.db","Web Data")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Python/Shell Reads Browser Credential Store (ChocoPoC Stealer)
id: 2f7c6a19-8d34-4b52-9e11-6c0a3f8b1d90
description: Detects python or shell accessing Chrome/Edge/Firefox credential and cookie stores or macOS Keychains, matching ChocoPoC's browser-secret collection.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-chocopoc-malware-targets-researchers-via-trojanized-poc-exploits/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/02
tags:
  - attack.t1555.003
  - attack.t1539
  - attack.t1555.001
logsource:
  category: file_access
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|contains:
      - 'python'
      - 'bash'
      - '/sh'
  selection_target:
    FileName|contains:
      - 'Login Data'
      - 'cookies.sqlite'
      - 'logins.json'
      - 'key4.db'
      - '/.config/google-chrome/'
      - '/.mozilla/firefox/'
      - '/.config/BraveSoftware/'
  condition: selection_proc and selection_target
level: high
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo
| ContextImageFileName=/(python3?|bash|sh)(\.exe)?$/i
| TargetFileName=/(Login Data|Cookies|Web Data|cookies\.sqlite|logins\.json|key4\.db|[\/\\]\.mozilla[\/\\]firefox[\/\\]|google-chrome|BraveSoftware|Keychains)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.process_name="python" OR Filesystem.process_name="python3" OR Filesystem.process_name="bash" OR Filesystem.process_name="sh") (Filesystem.file_name="Login Data" OR Filesystem.file_name="Cookies" OR Filesystem.file_name="Web Data" OR Filesystem.file_name="cookies.sqlite" OR Filesystem.file_name="logins.json" OR Filesystem.file_name="key4.db" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.mozilla/firefox/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.config/google-chrome/*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.process_name="python" OR Filesystem.process_name="python3" OR Filesystem.process_name="bash" OR Filesystem.process_name="sh") (Filesystem.file_name="Login Data" OR Filesystem.file_name="Cookies" OR Filesystem.file_name="Web Data" OR Filesystem.file_name="cookies.sqlite" OR Filesystem.file_name="logins.json" OR Filesystem.file_name="key4.db" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.mozilla/firefox/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.config/google-chrome/*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Python bulk enumeration of sensitive files (.md/.txt/.db/.sqlite) from PoC context AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a single Python process reading many distinct .md/.txt/.db/.sqlite files across ≥2 target types in a short window — matching ChocoPoC's stated search for text files, markdown docs and database files. Benign PoC execution does not sweep the filesystem for documentation and DB files. Rationale: Turns the article's explicit collection targets (text, markdown documentation, database files) into a per-process fan-out threshold gated to the python interpreter, which distinguishes a stealer sweep from ordinary PoC file I/O. No Sigma emitted — this is a count/threshold correlation, not single-event. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sekoia.com/blog • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chocopoc-malware-delivered-via-trojanized-poc-exploits/
ATT&CKT1083 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Python static-site/docs generator (mkdocs, sphinx) reading many .md files
  • Data pipeline ingesting many .db/.sqlite/.csv-adjacent files
  • pytest run touching fixture .txt/.db files
  • Backup or indexing script written in Python (e.g. desktop search)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("mkdocs","sphinx","pytest","jupyter","pelican","m>backup")
Response runbook
1) Triage: review InitiatingProcessCommandLine and working dir — is this a known docs/data tool, or an interpreter under site-packages/a cloned PoC? Inspect SampleFiles for sensitive content (creds, notes, DBs). 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate the host and kill the process before exfil completes; preserve the accessed file list. 3) Hunt: correlate the same process/host with UC3 Mapbox egress and UC4 browser-store access to confirm the full ChocoPoC chain, then sweep the fleet for the same fan-out pattern.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3")
| where FileName endswith ".md" or FileName endswith ".txt" or FileName endswith ".db" or FileName endswith ".sqlite" or FileName endswith ".sqlite3"
| extend Ext = tostring(extract(@"\.([^.]+)$", 1, FileName))
| summarize DistinctFiles=dcount(FolderPath), DistinctExtTypes=dcount(Ext), SampleFiles=make_set(FileName, 20), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where DistinctFiles >= 25 and DistinctExtTypes >= 2   // 25 = broad sweep across >=2 of the article's target types
| order by DistinctFiles desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3")
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("md","txt","db","sqlite","sqlite3")
| summarize DistinctFiles=dcount(TargetFilePath), DistinctExtTypes=dcount(TargetFileExtension), SampleFiles=make_set(TargetFileName, 20), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessId, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DistinctFiles >= 25 and DistinctExtTypes >= 2
| order by DistinctFiles desc
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo
| ContextImageFileName=/python3?(\.exe)?$/i
| TargetFileName=/\.(md|txt|db|sqlite3?)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextProcessId], function=count(as=FileCount))
| FileCount >= 25
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` dc(Filesystem.file_path) as DistinctFiles values(Filesystem.file_name) as sampleFiles min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.process_name="python" OR Filesystem.process_name="python3") (Filesystem.file_name="*.md" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.txt" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.db" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.sqlite" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.sqlite3") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_id _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where DistinctFiles>=25 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(Filesystem.file_path) as DistinctFiles values(Filesystem.file_name) as sampleFiles min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.process_name="python" OR Filesystem.process_name="python3") (Filesystem.file_name="*.md" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.txt" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.db" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.sqlite" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.sqlite3") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_id _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where DistinctFiles>=25 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user

Unpatched Argo CD Repo-Server Flaw Could Let Attackers Take Over Kubernetes Clusters

The Hacker News
2026-07-01 11 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Argo CD, a widely used tool for deploying software to Kubernetes, has an unpatched flaw in its repo-server component that lets an unauthenticated attacker run code, provided they can reach the component's internal network port. Synacktiv, which found the bug, says it can lead to a full cluster takeover. There is no fix and no CVE. The firm says it reported the flaw to Argo CD's maintainers in

Argo CD repo-server exploit: kustomize --helm-command points to non-helm script AIExploitation High
Hunts the Synacktiv unauthenticated RCE against Argo CD repo-server, where an attacker sets kustomize's --helm-command to an attacker-supplied script (pulled from a rogue Git repo) instead of the helm binary. Fires when a kustomize process runs with --helm-command whose target does not resolve to helm. Rationale: Uses the article's exact exploit primitive — kustomize's --helm-command re-pointed away from the helm binary. Cross-checked with Synacktiv reporting relayed via The Hacker News; legitimate kustomize-with-helm always calls a path ending in 'helm', so a non-helm target is high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html • https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user-guide/kustomize/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate custom kustomize helm plugin wrapper script that ends in something other than 'helm' (e.g. a vendored 'helm-wrapper.sh')
  • In-house CI that shims helm via a shell script for private OCI auth
  • Config Management Plugin (CMP) that legitimately templates via a custom binary
  • Debugging/troubleshooting by a platform engineer manually running kustomize with a custom helm path
Suppression filter
| where HelmCmd !in~ ("/custom/bin/helm-wrapper.sh") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("argocd-repo-server","kustomize")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full ProcessCommandLine and the value of --helm-command; confirm whether the target is an approved helm binary path or an unexpected script/temp path. Identify the host — it should be an argocd-repo-server pod/node. 2) Contain: cordon the node, kill the repo-server pod, and apply the Argo CD network policies (networkPolicy.create=true) so only Argo CD components can reach repo-server (TCP 8081) and Redis (6379). Rotate the Redis password. 3) Hunt: review DeviceNetworkEvents from repo-server for egress to attacker Git/registry, check Redis 'mfst' cache integrity, and audit recently synced Applications for attacker-supplied workloads.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--helm-command"
| extend HelmCmd = extract(@"--helm-command[=\s]+([^\s]+)", 1, ProcessCommandLine)
| where isnotempty(HelmCmd)
| where HelmCmd !endswith "helm" and HelmCmd !endswith "helm.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, HelmCmd, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "--helm-command"
| extend HelmCmd = extract(@"--helm-command[=\s]+([^\s]+)", 1, TargetProcessCommandLine)
| where isnotempty(HelmCmd) and HelmCmd !endswith "helm"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, HelmCmd, TargetProcessCommandLine

Argo CD repo-server / kustomize spawning shell or network tooling AIExploitation High
Detects code execution on the Argo CD repo-server: the parent process argocd-repo-server or kustomize spawning an interactive shell or network utility (sh, bash, curl, wget, nc, python). This is the observable outcome of the --helm-command RCE where an attacker-controlled script runs in place of helm. Rationale: The repo-server normally only execs git, helm, kustomize and gpg; a shell or curl/wget/nc child is the direct execution artifact of the article's script-injection RCE. Parent-child pairing keeps this far tighter than a bare LOLBin hunt. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html • https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/operator-manual/security/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1610
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom Config Management Plugins that legitimately shell out to curl/python for private repo auth
  • Init scripts or entrypoint wrappers baked into a custom repo-server image
  • Helm hooks or pre-render scripts that fetch dependency charts via curl/wget
  • Platform-engineer debugging inside the repo-server pod via kubectl exec (would show sh/bash)
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "registry-1.docker.io")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child ProcessCommandLine and grandparent chain; confirm it is not a known CMP or debugging session (correlate with kubectl exec / DeviceLogonEvents). 2) Contain: kill the repo-server pod, enable Argo CD network policies, and block the repo-server pod's egress to any non-Git/non-Redis destination. 3) Hunt: pivot to the destination IP/URL of any curl/wget, check for a subsequent Redis connection and cache 'mfst' modification, and review new Applications synced after the event.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("argocd-repo-server","kustomize")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","python","python3","nc","ncat","busybox")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName in~ ("argocd-repo-server","kustomize")
| where TargetProcessName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","python","python3","nc","ncat","busybox")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine

Argo CD service account deploys privileged / host-escape workload AIInstallation High
Detects the cluster-takeover payload: after poisoning the Argo CD Redis cache, the Argo CD service account syncs a workload whose pod spec requests privileged mode, hostPID/hostNetwork/hostIPC, or a hostPath mount of the Docker/container socket. Targets the Kubernetes API audit trail of the malicious manifest being applied. Rationale: Ties the article's outcome ('Argo CD deployed an attacker-supplied workload') to the concrete host-escape primitives (privileged, hostPID, docker.sock) that a takeover payload needs, scoped to the Argo CD service account as the requestor so normal privileged system pods don't match. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html • https://cycode.com/blog/revealing-argo-cd-critical-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1610 T1072
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate privileged DaemonSets (CNI, CSI, node-exporter, Falco) that Argo CD genuinely manages via GitOps
  • A platform team intentionally deploying a privileged monitoring agent through Argo CD
  • hostNetwork ingress controllers deployed by Argo CD
  • Cluster bootstrap/app-of-apps sync that includes system components with hostPath mounts
Suppression filter
| where Namespace !in ("kube-system","monitoring","argocd") and not (Name has_any ("cni","csi","node-exporter","falco","ingress"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: diff the offending manifest against the Git source of truth — if the privileged spec is not in the declared repo, it is Redis cache poisoning. Confirm the source Application and repoURL. 2) Contain: pause auto-sync on the affected Application, delete the malicious workload, rotate the Redis password, and enable network policies isolating repo-server/Redis. 3) Hunt: enumerate all pods created by the argocd SA in the window, check for reverse shells / crypto miners in those pods, and validate no ClusterRoleBinding was added for the argocd SA.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| extend Res = tostring(ObjectRef.resource)
| where Res in ("pods","deployments","daemonsets","statefulsets","replicasets")
| extend Requestor = tostring(Username)
| where Requestor has "argocd"
| extend ReqStr = tostring(RequestObject)
| where ReqStr has_any ('"privileged":true','"hostPID":true','"hostNetwork":true','"hostIPC":true','/var/run/docker.sock','/var/run/crio/crio.sock','"hostPath"')
| project TimeGenerated, Requestor, Verb, Res, Namespace=tostring(ObjectRef.namespace), Name=tostring(ObjectRef.name), UserAgent, RequestUri

ClusterRoleBinding granting elevated rights to Argo CD service account AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects post-compromise privilege escalation where a RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding is created referencing an Argo CD service account and grants cluster-admin or wildcard verbs, consolidating the 'full cluster takeover' the article warns about. Targets the Kubernetes RBAC audit trail. Rationale: The article's stated impact is 'full cluster takeover', which requires elevated RBAC; a new binding tying the argocd SA to cluster-admin is the highest-fidelity signal of that escalation and rarely happens outside of initial install. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9766-5277-j5hr
ATT&CKT1098 T1548
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Initial Argo CD install/upgrade via Helm that legitimately binds the argocd application-controller to broad roles
  • GitOps-managed RBAC where the argocd SA role is declared in Git and reconciled
  • Platform team intentionally granting Argo CD cluster-admin for multi-cluster management
  • Disaster-recovery re-provisioning of the Argo CD namespace
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has "helm" and Requestor !has "system:serviceaccount:kube-system"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify who (user.username / UserAgent) created the binding — an install via 'helm'/'argocd' user agent during a maintenance window is likely benign; an ad-hoc kubectl or the argocd SA itself creating its own escalation is not. 2) Contain: delete the offending ClusterRoleBinding, revoke/rotate the argocd SA token, and enable network policies. 3) Hunt: review all actions taken by the argocd SA after the binding, enumerate new workloads and secrets accessed, and check Redis cache integrity.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| extend Res = tostring(ObjectRef.resource)
| where Res in ("clusterrolebindings","rolebindings")
| extend ReqStr = tostring(RequestObject)
| where ReqStr has_any ("argocd","argo-cd")
| where ReqStr has_any ("cluster-admin","\"verbs\":[\"*\"]","\"*\"")
| project TimeGenerated, Requestor=tostring(Username), Verb, Res, Name=tostring(ObjectRef.name), UserAgent, RequestObject

New Argo CD Application/ApplicationSet pointing to external Git repo AIInstallation Medium
Hunts persistence via a backdoored Argo CD Application: creation or mutation of an applications.argoproj.io / applicationsets.argoproj.io resource whose source repoURL points at an external or untrusted Git host, which would let an attacker continuously reconcile malicious manifests into the cluster. Surfaces the repoURL for analyst triage against the org allowlist. Rationale: The attack reconciles workloads from an attacker-controlled Git repo; monitoring Application/ApplicationSet CRD writes and surfacing repoURL lets analysts spot a source pointed at an untrusted host. Left as hunting because the trusted-repo allowlist is org-specific and cannot be hardcoded. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html • https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/operator-manual/security/
ATT&CKT1525 T1072
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Routine GitOps onboarding of a new legitimate Application by the platform team
  • App-of-apps pattern generating many child Applications from a template
  • Developers self-servicing new Applications pointed at approved internal GitLab/GitHub Enterprise
  • Migration of Applications between repos during a repo consolidation
Response runbook
1) Triage: compare RepoURL against the approved Git host allowlist; a public/raw-IP or newly registered domain source is suspicious. Confirm who created it (Requestor/UserAgent). 2) Contain: pause auto-sync and delete the Application if the repo is untrusted; enable network policies. 3) Hunt: inspect the manifests that repo would render (privileged specs, external images), correlate with UC3/UC4, and rotate Argo CD repo credentials given CVE-2025-55190/CVE-2026-42880 secret-exposure history.

| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| extend Res = tostring(ObjectRef.resource)
| where Res in ("applications","applicationsets")
| extend RepoURL = tostring(RequestObject.spec.source.repoURL)
| extend RepoSources = tostring(RequestObject.spec.sources)
| extend RepoTemplate = tostring(RequestObject.spec.template.spec.source.repoURL)
| where isnotempty(RepoURL) or isnotempty(RepoSources) or isnotempty(RepoTemplate)
| project TimeGenerated, Requestor=tostring(Username), Verb, Res, AppName=tostring(ObjectRef.name), RepoURL, RepoTemplate, RepoSources, UserAgent

index=* sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" verb IN ("create","update","patch") "objectRef.resource" IN ("applications","applicationsets") | spath | eval repoURL=coalesce('requestObject.spec.source.repoURL','requestObject.spec.template.spec.source.repoURL') | where isnotnull(repoURL) | table _time user.username verb objectRef.namespace objectRef.name repoURL

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2024-31989", "CVE-2025-55190", "CVE-2026-42880")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2024-31989", "CVE-2025-55190", "CVE-2026-42880")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2024-31989", "CVE-2025-55190", "CVE-2026-42880")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
