Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Suspicious MFA Bypass or MFA Reset Activity · [LLM] Credential Stuffing and Brute Force Against Enterprise Accounts · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Lateral Movement via Valid Compromised Credentials · [LLM] Reconnaissance and Information Gathering Pre-Exploitation · [LLM] Bulk data staging and exfiltration via MEGA / rclone · [LLM] Adversary lurking in incident-response chat tools and calls · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Suspicious MFA Bypass or MFA Reset Activity AIExploitation Medium
Hunts Scattered Spider's signature MFA-fatigue / push-bombing pattern: a burst of rejected MFA challenges for a single user followed shortly by a successful sign-in, indicating the user (or a help-desk-reset factor) eventually approved an attacker-driven prompt. Article-specific because the crew's core play is talking help desks into resetting/approving logins rather than breaking software. Rationale: Uses the exact Entra/Azure AD MFA-denied result code 500121 followed by a success inside the same fatigue window — the documented Scattered Spider push-bombing + help-desk-reset signature (CISA AA23-320A). Threshold of 5 rejects/hr is above legitimate user behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1015/
ATT&CKT1621 T1556.006
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User genuinely mis-taps 'Deny' several times on a real prompt before approving
  • Authenticator app time-drift causing repeated failed OTP entries then a correct one
  • Shared/service account where multiple humans trigger prompts for the same identity
  • Poor cellular connectivity dropping push notifications until a retry succeeds
  • Newly enrolled device where the user fumbles first-time MFA setup
Suppression filter
| where IPAddress !in (dynamic(["<corp egress IPs are known-good; add tenant CIDRs>"])) | where Country !in ("<home country>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the AccountUpn's sign-in log around FirstDenial–SuccessTime; check the success IPAddress/Country vs the user's baseline and whether a help-desk password/MFA reset preceded it in AuditLogs. 2) Contain: if the success came from a new IP/geo or an unrecognised device, revoke sessions (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), require password reset, and re-verify the MFA method the user actually controls. 3) Hunt: search AuditLogs for 'Update user'/'security info registered' on the same account, and pivot to any post-auth Teams/SharePoint access from the suspicious IP.
let denials = AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ErrorCode == 500121   // MFA denied / not completed = push-bombing
| summarize DenialCount = count(), FirstDenial = min(Timestamp), LastDenial = max(Timestamp) by AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where DenialCount >= 5;      // 5 rejected pushes/hr = fatigue attempt (P99 legit <=2)
let successes = AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| project SuccessTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Country;
denials
| join kind=inner successes on AccountUpn
| where SuccessTime between (FirstDenial .. LastDenial + 30m)
| project AccountUpn, FirstDenial, LastDenial, DenialCount, SuccessTime, IPAddress, Country
| order by LastDenial desc
let denials = SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "500121"   // MFA denied / not completed
| summarize DenialCount = count(), FirstDenial = min(TimeGenerated), LastDenial = max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DenialCount >= 5;
let successes = SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "0"
| project SuccessTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, LocationDetails;
denials
| join kind=inner successes on UserPrincipalName
| where SuccessTime between (FirstDenial .. LastDenial + 30m)
| project UserPrincipalName, FirstDenial, LastDenial, DenialCount, SuccessTime, IPAddress, LocationDetails
| order by LastDenial desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.status.errorCode:500121
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action=failure Authentication.signature_id="500121" by Authentication.user _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | rename count as DenialCount | where DenialCount>=5 | join type=inner user [| tstats `summariesonly` min(_time) as SuccessTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action=success by Authentication.user Authentication.src | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`] | where SuccessTime>=_time AND SuccessTime<=(_time+5400) | table user DenialCount SuccessTime src
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action=failure Authentication.signature_id="500121" by Authentication.user _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | rename count as DenialCount | where DenialCount>=5 | join type=inner user [| tstats summariesonly=false min(_time) as SuccessTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action=success by Authentication.user Authentication.src | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`] | where SuccessTime>=_time AND SuccessTime<=(_time+5400) | table user DenialCount SuccessTime src
Credential Stuffing and Brute Force Against Enterprise Accounts AIExploitation Medium
Detects password-spray / credential-stuffing bursts against Entra ID: a single source IP producing invalid-credential failures across many distinct user accounts within an hour. Grounds the article's 'hacking charges' and the group's documented large-scale credential abuse into an actionable identity detection. Rationale: Pivots on Entra failure code 50126 (bad credentials) aggregated by source IP with a distinct-user fan-out threshold — the canonical spray shape. 20 distinct victims/IP/hr is well above any single legitimate misconfigured client. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1015/
ATT&CKT1110.003 T1110.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Misconfigured on-prem app or MFA server retrying stale creds for many mailboxes from one NAT egress
  • Corporate VPN/NAT gateway aggregating many users behind one IP after a mass password expiry
  • Legacy IMAP/POP client farm with cached bad passwords post rotation
  • Pen-test / red-team password-spray engagement
  • SSO migration causing bulk auth failures from a single connector IP
Suppression filter
| where IPAddress !in (dynamic(["<corp NAT/VPN egress CIDRs>"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the source IP's ASN/geo and whether it matches a known corporate egress; list the targeted users and check if any subsequently succeeded from the same IP. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the identity provider / Conditional Access named-location, and force reset on any account that authenticated successfully from it. 3) Hunt: search for the same IP in successful sign-ins (ResultType 0) and for follow-on MFA-registration or Teams/SharePoint access from those sessions.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ErrorCode == 50126   // invalid username or password
| summarize TargetedUsers = dcount(AccountUpn), FailedAttempts = count(), Users = make_set(AccountUpn, 50) by IPAddress, Country, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where TargetedUsers >= 20   // >=20 distinct users sprayed from one IP/hr
| order by TargetedUsers desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "50126"   // invalid username or password
| summarize TargetedUsers = dcount(UserPrincipalName), FailedAttempts = count(), Users = make_set(UserPrincipalName, 50) by IPAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where TargetedUsers >= 20
| order by TargetedUsers desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.status.errorCode:(50126 OR 50053 OR 50055)
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` dc(Authentication.user) as TargetedUsers count as FailedAttempts from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action=failure Authentication.signature_id="50126" by Authentication.src _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where TargetedUsers>=20 | sort - TargetedUsers
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(Authentication.user) as TargetedUsers count as FailedAttempts from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action=failure Authentication.signature_id="50126" by Authentication.src _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where TargetedUsers>=20 | sort - TargetedUsers
Lateral Movement via Valid Compromised Credentials AIActions on Objectives Medium
Surfaces post-compromise use of valid credentials by flagging a single account that successfully signs in from multiple distinct IPs or countries within a short window — the impossible-travel / concurrent-session pattern Scattered Spider produces once inside. Complements the credential-access detections by catching the movement that follows a help-desk-driven reset. Rationale: Anti-baseline of successful (ResultType 0) sign-ins fanning out across IPs/countries per account per hour is the cleanest 'stolen valid credential in active use' signal; no invented columns, works on both Entra schemas. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1015/
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1021.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User on corporate VPN/ZTNA that egresses through multiple regional PoPs
  • Mobile user roaming between cellular and Wi-Fi networks with different public IPs
  • Legitimate frequent traveller or a user plus their MDM-managed devices in different networks
  • Cloud/SaaS service accessing on the user's behalf from datacentre IPs
  • Household with dual-stack IPv4/IPv6 flipping public addresses
Suppression filter
| where IPs !has_any ("<corporate VPN egress CIDRs>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: map each IP to ASN/geo and device; confirm whether the geos are physically reconcilable and whether any IP is a hosting/VPN provider common to Scattered Spider. 2) Contain: revoke sessions and require re-auth with a phishing-resistant method; if a hosting-provider IP is present, block it via Conditional Access. 3) Hunt: from the suspect IP/session, pivot to DeviceLogonEvents for RDP/SSH (LogonType RemoteInteractive) into sensitive hosts and to any privileged-role assignment in AuditLogs.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| summarize IPCount = dcount(IPAddress), CountryCount = dcount(Country), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20), Countries = make_set(Country, 20) by AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where CountryCount >= 2 or IPCount >= 5   // same account, many geos/IPs within an hour
| order by IPCount desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "0"
| extend Country = tostring(parse_json(tostring(LocationDetails)).countryOrRegion)
| summarize IPCount = dcount(IPAddress), CountryCount = dcount(Country), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20), Countries = make_set(Country, 20) by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where CountryCount >= 2 or IPCount >= 5
| order by IPCount desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` dc(Authentication.src) as IPCount values(Authentication.src) as IPs from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action=success by Authentication.user _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where IPCount>=5 | sort - IPCount
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(Authentication.src) as IPCount values(Authentication.src) as IPs from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action=success by Authentication.user _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where IPCount>=5 | sort - IPCount
Reconnaissance and Information Gathering Pre-Exploitation AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a burst of internal directory/domain enumeration (net group, nltest, adfind, Get-AD* cmdlets) from a single interactive user account — the recon Scattered Spider runs after gaining a foothold to locate admins and sensitive shares. Hunts the specific reconnaissance tooling, not generic PowerShell use. Rationale: Ties named recon binaries (nltest, adfind) and specific Get-AD* cmdlets to a per-user hourly burst threshold, excluding machine accounts — high-signal for hands-on-keyboard enumeration rather than routine admin scripting. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1015/
ATT&CKT1087.002 T1482
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin or helpdesk running net group / Get-ADGroupMember for legitimate access reviews
  • Monitoring/IAM tooling enumerating AD on a schedule under a service account
  • SCCM/Intune or vulnerability scanner performing domain discovery
  • Onboarding scripts querying groups for new-hire provisioning
  • Security team's own AD-audit tooling (e.g. PingCastle, BloodHound collector by IT)
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("<sanctioned admin/service accounts>") | where DeviceName !in~ ("<known admin jump hosts>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the AccountName is a sanctioned admin/service identity and whether the host is an admin jump box; review the full command set for trust/DC enumeration. 2) Contain: if the account is a standard user, disable it and isolate the device pending review. 3) Hunt: pivot from the same account/host to subsequent lateral logons, credential-access tooling, and archive/exfil binaries (rclone, 7z) to place this recon in a kill chain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName in~ ("net.exe","net1.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("group \"domain admins\"","group /domain","user /domain","group \"enterprise admins\""))
    or (FileName =~ "nltest.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/domain_trusts","/dclist","/trusted_domains"))
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Get-ADUser","Get-ADGroup","Get-ADGroupMember","Get-ADComputer","Get-ADDomainController"))
    or (FileName =~ "adfind.exe")
| summarize CmdCount = count(), Cmds = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 20), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, AccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where CmdCount >= 5   // burst of directory recon in one hour
| order by CmdCount desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| extend Proc = tolower(NewProcessName)
| where (Proc endswith "\\net.exe" or Proc endswith "\\net1.exe") and CommandLine has_any ("group \"domain admins\"","group /domain","user /domain")
    or Proc endswith "\\nltest.exe" and CommandLine has_any ("/domain_trusts","/dclist")
    or (Proc endswith "\\powershell.exe" or Proc endswith "\\pwsh.exe") and CommandLine has_any ("Get-ADUser","Get-ADGroup","Get-ADComputer","Get-ADDomainController")
    or Proc endswith "\\adfind.exe"
| summarize CmdCount = count(), Cmds = make_set(CommandLine, 20) by Computer, SubjectUserName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where CmdCount >= 5
| order by CmdCount desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:(*\\net.exe OR *\\net1.exe OR *\\nltest.exe OR *\\adfind.exe OR *\\NET.EXE OR *\\NLTEST.EXE OR *\\ADFIND.EXE) OR (@Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe) AND @CommandLine:(*Get-ADUser* OR *Get-ADGroup* OR *Get-ADComputer*)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (ImageFileName=/\\(net|net1|nltest|adfind)\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/(\/domain|domain admins|domain_trusts|\/dclist)/i) OR (ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/Get-AD(User|Group|GroupMember|Computer|DomainController)/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName], function=count())
| _count >= 5
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Processes.process) as Cmds from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("net.exe","net1.exe","nltest.exe","adfind.exe") OR (Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process IN ("*Get-ADUser*","*Get-ADGroup*","*Get-ADComputer*","*Get-ADDomainController*"))) AND NOT Processes.user IN ("*$") by Processes.dest Processes.user _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where count>=5 | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Processes.process) as Cmds from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("net.exe","net1.exe","nltest.exe","adfind.exe") OR (Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process IN ("*Get-ADUser*","*Get-ADGroup*","*Get-ADComputer*","*Get-ADDomainController*"))) AND NOT Processes.user IN ("*$") by Processes.dest Processes.user _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where count>=5 | sort - count
Bulk data staging and exfiltration via MEGA / rclone AIActions on Objectives High
Detects Scattered Spider's documented exfiltration tooling — rclone and MEGA clients, plus password-protected archive creation with 7-Zip/WinRAR — used to stage and move copied corporate data before extortion. Directly supports the article's account of intruders copying a retailer's data and demanding ~$8M. Rationale: rclone and MEGA (megacmd/MEGAsync) are explicitly named Scattered Spider exfil tools in CISA AA23-320A; pairing them with password-protected archive flags (-hp/-p/-mx) keys the article's 'copied its data' claim to concrete, rare-in-user-space binaries. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1015/
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1560.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT team legitimately using rclone for sanctioned cloud backup/migration
  • Developers or users making password-protected 7-Zip/WinRAR archives for routine transfers
  • Backup software invoking Compress-Archive in scheduled jobs
  • A user with a personal MEGAsync install syncing non-corporate files
  • DevOps pipelines archiving build artifacts with -mx compression
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("<sanctioned backup/migration operators>") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("<approved backup agent>.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the command line for the remote target (rclone 'mega:'/'remote:' config, archive output path) and correlate with DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound connections to mega.nz / user.mega.co.nz. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and block MEGA/rclone destinations at the proxy/firewall; preserve the staged archive for scoping. 3) Hunt: identify which shares/DBs were read before the archive, check for the same tool on other hosts, and review the initiating account for a preceding help-desk reset or anomalous sign-in.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("rclone.exe","megacmd.exe","megasync.exe","mega.exe")
    or (FileName in~ ("7z.exe","7za.exe","winrar.exe","rar.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any (" a "," -hp"," -p ","-mx"))
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "Compress-Archive")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| extend Proc = tolower(NewProcessName)
| where Proc has_any ("\\rclone.exe","\\megacmd.exe","\\megasync.exe","\\mega.exe")
    or (Proc has_any ("\\7z.exe","\\7za.exe","\\winrar.exe","\\rar.exe") and CommandLine has_any (" a "," -hp"," -p ","-mx"))
    or (Proc has_any ("\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe") and CommandLine has "Compress-Archive")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Scattered Spider Data Exfiltration Tooling (rclone/MEGA/archive)
id: 7f3c1e2a-8b4d-4c6e-9a1f-2d5b6c7e8f90
status: experimental
description: Detects execution of rclone, MEGA clients or password-protected archive creation used by Scattered Spider for bulk data staging and exfiltration.
references:
  - https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/19-year-old-scattered-spider-suspect.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/02
tags:
  - attack.exfiltration
  - attack.t1567.002
  - attack.t1560.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_tools:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\rclone.exe'
      - '\megacmd.exe'
      - '\megasync.exe'
      - '\mega.exe'
  selection_archive:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\7z.exe'
      - '\7za.exe'
      - '\winrar.exe'
      - '\rar.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - ' -hp'
      - ' -p '
      - '-mx'
  condition: selection_tools or selection_archive
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:(*\\rclone.exe OR *\\Rclone.exe OR *\\megacmd.exe OR *\\MEGAcmd.exe OR *\\megasync.exe OR *\\MEGAsync.exe OR *\\mega.exe) OR (@Image:(*\\7z.exe OR *\\7za.exe OR *\\winrar.exe OR *\\WinRAR.exe OR *\\rar.exe) AND @CommandLine:(* a * OR *\-hp* OR *\-mx*)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (ImageFileName=/\\(rclone|megacmd|megasync|mega)\.exe$/i) OR (ImageFileName=/\\(7z|7za|winrar|rar)\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/\s(a|-hp|-p|-mx)/i) OR (ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/Compress-Archive/i)
| table([_time, aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Processes.process) as Cmds min(_time) as firstTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("rclone.exe","megacmd.exe","megasync.exe","mega.exe") OR (Processes.process_name IN ("7z.exe","7za.exe","winrar.exe","rar.exe") AND Processes.process IN ("* a *","*-hp*","*-p *","*-mx*")) OR (Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process="*Compress-Archive*")) AND NOT Processes.user IN ("*$") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort - firstTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Processes.process) as Cmds min(_time) as firstTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("rclone.exe","megacmd.exe","megasync.exe","mega.exe") OR (Processes.process_name IN ("7z.exe","7za.exe","winrar.exe","rar.exe") AND Processes.process IN ("* a *","*-hp*","*-p *","*-mx*")) OR (Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process="*Compress-Archive*")) AND NOT Processes.user IN ("*$") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort - firstTime
Adversary lurking in incident-response chat tools and calls AIActions on Objectives Low
Hunts the article's distinctive Scattered Spider tradecraft: once inside, intruders lurk in the victim's collaboration tools and join breach-response meetings to watch defenders. Flags an account reading/listing messages across an unusually large number of distinct Teams channels/chats in a short window — collection of IR chatter rather than normal use. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's specific claim that intruders 'lurk in a company's chat tools and join the calls it holds to respond to the breach'; a per-account hourly fan-out across many Teams objects is an abnormal collection pattern distinct from routine messaging. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1015/
ATT&CKT1213.005 T1580
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Compliance/eDiscovery or DLP tooling enumerating Teams content under a service account
  • A community manager or exec assistant who legitimately monitors many channels
  • Teams admin performing a migration or bulk export
  • Automated bot/connector indexing messages for search
  • New employee catching up across many onboarding channels on day one
Suppression filter
| where AccountDisplayName !in~ ("<eDiscovery/compliance service accounts>","<Teams admin accounts>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the account is a sanctioned compliance/admin/bot identity; review which channels were accessed — flag any named 'incident', 'IR', 'breach', or exec crisis channels. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, revoke Teams sessions, disable the account, and move breach-response coordination to an out-of-band channel the adversary cannot see. 3) Hunt: correlate the account with a preceding help-desk MFA reset or anomalous sign-in, and check for guest/external members recently added to IR channels.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType in ("MessagesListed","MessageRead","ChatRetrieved","MeetingParticipantDetail")
| summarize DistinctObjects = dcount(ObjectId), Ops = count(), Actions = make_set(ActionType, 10) by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where DistinctObjects >= 15   // reading across >=15 channels/chats in an hour = harvesting
| order by DistinctObjects desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in ("MessagesListed","MessageRead","ChatRetrieved","MeetingParticipantDetail","MemberAdded")
| summarize DistinctChannels = dcount(ObjectId), Ops = count(), OpSet = make_set(Operation, 10) by UserId, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctChannels >= 15
| order by DistinctChannels desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] tj-actions/changed-files malicious commit 0e58ed86 referenced on host (CVE-2025-30066)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] GitHub Actions runner outbound to gist.githubusercontent.com (tj-actions/changed-files CVE-2025-30066)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
GitHub Actions runner outbound to gist.githubusercontent.com (tj-actions/changed-files CVE-2025-30066) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts a self-hosted CI/CD runner process (Runner.Worker/node/python/curl) reaching gist.githubusercontent.com — the exact egress the compromised tj-actions/changed-files action used to pull its memory-dumping Python second stage. This was StepSecurity Harden-Runner's original detection signal for the March 2025 incident. Rationale: Uses the corroborated network IOC (outbound to gist.githubusercontent.com from a runner) that StepSecurity's Harden-Runner used to detect CVE-2025-30066; scoped to runner process ancestry (Runner.Worker/node/python/_actions paths) to separate it from ordinary developer gist fetches. Cross-checked against CISA, Wiz and Sysdig write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2025/03/18/supply-chain-compromise-third-party-tj-actionschanged-files-cve-2025-30066-and-reviewdogaction • https://www.wiz.io/blog/github-action-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066 • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/detecting-and-mitigating-the-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066
ATT&CKT1105 T1195.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A build step legitimately curls a config/install script hosted on a GitHub gist
  • Developer tooling or dotfiles bootstrap that pulls from gist.githubusercontent.com on a self-hosted runner
  • Package post-install hooks fetching helper scripts from a gist
  • Security tooling / EDR test harness deliberately reaching gist domains
  • Renovate/Dependabot-style automation resolving raw gist content
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("renovate","dependabot") or RemoteUrl has "raw.githubusercontent.com/your-org")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full command line and parent chain of the initiating process; confirm it ran inside a GitHub Actions job (Runner.Worker/_work/_actions path) and identify the workflow/repo. Grab the exact gist URL and the resolved IP. 2) Contain: if the job used tj-actions/changed-files (or any action pinned to a mutable tag), pause the runner, and immediately rotate every secret exposed to workflows that ran between 2025-03-12 00:00 and 2025-03-15 12:00 UTC (access keys, GitHub PATs, npm tokens, RSA keys). 3) Hunt: search the same runner fleet for the malicious commit 0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67 and for double-base64 blobs written to workflow logs; review runner egress for other first-seen domains.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "gist.githubusercontent.com" or RemoteUrl has "gist.github.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","python.exe","python3","python","curl.exe","curl","wget","Runner.Worker.exe","Runner.Worker")
     or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("Runner.Worker.exe","Runner.Worker","node.exe","node")
     or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("actions-runner","_work","_actions")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "gist.githubusercontent.com" or HttpHostName in~ ("gist.githubusercontent.com","gist.github.com")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpHostName, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: GitHub Actions Runner Outbound to GitHub Gist (tj-actions CVE-2025-30066)
id: 6f2a1c84-9d3e-4f7a-b0c1-2e5a8d4f9b31
description: A GitHub Actions runner-context process connecting to gist.githubusercontent.com, matching the second-stage payload fetch of the compromised tj-actions/changed-files action.

tj-actions/changed-files malicious commit 0e58ed86 referenced on host (CVE-2025-30066) AIDelivery High
Alerts on the exact malicious tj-actions/changed-files commit SHA (0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67) appearing in any process command line or file path on a self-hosted runner — i.e. the compromised action being fetched, checked out, or pinned. A pure, second-source-confirmed IOC hunt for the retagged supply-chain payload. Rationale: Uses the article's SHA1 (0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67), independently confirmed by CISA and the GitHub Advisory as the single malicious commit every tj-actions/changed-files tag (v1.0.0–v44.5.1) was pointed to — a unique, zero-ambiguity IOC that only appears when the compromised action is fetched, checked out, or SHA-pinned. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/ghsa-mrrh-fwg8-r2c3 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2025/03/18/supply-chain-compromise-third-party-tj-actionschanged-files-cve-2025-30066-and-reviewdogaction • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/github-actions-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC/threat-intel tooling scanning for the hash as an IOC (grep, EDR IOC sweep) surfaces the string in its own command line
  • A remediation script that greps repos/workflows for the malicious SHA
  • Vulnerability-management agent enumerating the commit as data
  • A security researcher reproducing/analyzing the incident in a lab runner
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("grep.exe","findstr.exe","rg.exe","select-string") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("IOC","threat-intel","scan-"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SHA appears in a real action fetch/checkout (Runner.Worker/git/_actions context) versus an analyst's own IOC-scan process; identify the repo and the workflow run time. 2) Contain: treat the runner and any workflow that executed the action as compromised — rotate all secrets exposed to workflows run between 2025-03-12 00:00 and 2025-03-15 12:00 UTC, and repin tj-actions/changed-files to the patched v46.0.1 by full SHA. 3) Hunt: pivot to outbound gist.githubusercontent.com egress from the same runner, inspect workflow logs for double-base64 secret blobs, and check for the sibling reviewdog/action-setup CVE-2025-30154 across the fleet.
let ioc = "0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67";
union
 (DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has ioc or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has ioc
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="ProcessEvent", Account=AccountName, Evidence=ProcessCommandLine, Context=InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
 (DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(90d)

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67") or SHA1 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67") or MD5 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67") or SHA1 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67") or MD5 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Machine that pulled compromised easy-day-js npm package (node_modules write) AIInstallation High
Identifies every developer laptop or CI runner that installed the malicious easy-day-js typosquat by detecting file writes into a node_modules\easy-day-js\ directory by a package manager. This directly answers the article's 'which machine pulled the compromised package' question and scopes the blast radius of the @mastra supply-chain compromise. Rationale: Anchors on the exact malicious package path node_modules\easy-day-js\ named in the article and confirmed by Microsoft/JFrog/Socket; any write there means that host resolved and installed the poisoned dependency, which is the precise blast-radius scoping signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://research.jfrog.com/post/easy-day-js/ • https://socket.dev/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher intentionally installing easy-day-js in a sandbox for analysis
  • An internal mirror/artifact-cache pre-fetching the package for quarantine before the removal
  • A CI job replaying an old lockfile that still references the malicious version during remediation testing
  • A developer restoring a git branch created before the compromise was disclosed
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "quarantine" and InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("malwareanalysis","sandbox")
Response runbook
1) Triage: from the hit, note DeviceName + account and pull the exact easy-day-js version written (check package.json under the folder); anything resolving 1.11.22 is malicious. 2) Contain: isolate the host from the network, kill node/npm processes, and delete the node_modules\easy-day-js tree; rotate any npm/registry tokens and cloud creds that lived on that host. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2/UC3 on the same DeviceName for outbound connections to 23.254.164.92/123 and for .pkg_history/.pkg_logs temp artifacts to confirm second-stage execution.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\node_modules\easy-day-js\"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","npx.cmd","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe","node")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Files=make_set(FileName, 20), any(SHA256) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "node_modules/easy-day-js" or TargetFilePath has @"node_modules\easy-day-js"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","npm","pnpm","yarn","npx")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Files=make_set(TargetFileName, 20) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath
| order by LastSeen desc

easy-day-js dropper C2 beacon to Sapphire Sleet Hostwinds infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Detects outbound connections from a package-manager/node process to the confirmed easy-day-js command-and-control hosts 23.254.164.92:8000 (payload delivery) and 23.254.164.123:443 (RAT C2). Presence of this traffic confirms the postinstall dropper executed and reached its second stage. Rationale: The two IPs, ports (8000/443) and /24 are confirmed by Microsoft and JFrog as the easy-day-js payload-delivery and RAT C2 endpoints; direct IP hits are unambiguous second-stage confirmation and near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://research.jfrog.com/post/easy-day-js/ • https://www.ox.security/blog/easy-day-js-supply-chain-attack-hits-mastra-ai-in-npm/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel or IR team actively sandbox-detonating the sample and letting it beacon
  • A honeypot/deception host deliberately allowed to reach the C2
  • Perimeter proxy/EDR test traffic validating that the block rule works
  • Shared-hosting neighbour on 23.254.164.0/24 unrelated to the campaign (mitigated by matching the two exact IPs, not the /24)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("sandbox","detonation") or DeviceName has "honeypot")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess making the connection — node.exe/npm during an install window strongly confirms true positive; capture RemotePort (8000=stage-2 fetch, 443=RAT beacon). 2) Contain: block 23.254.164.92 and 23.254.164.123 at the perimeter, isolate the host, and terminate the beaconing process. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for connections to 23.254.164.0/24 and correlate with UC1 node_modules\easy-day-js writes; rotate every credential/token that resided on beaconing hosts (assume infostealer collection succeeded).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("23.254.164.92","23.254.164.123")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("23.254.164.92","23.254.164.123")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

easy-day-js self-deleting postinstall dropper temp artifacts (.pkg_history/.pkg_logs) AIInstallation High
Detects creation of the .pkg_history / .pkg_logs marker files the easy-day-js dropper writes to the temp directory, and the self-delete pattern of a dropped .js payload during an npm install. These artifacts survive the dropper's evidence-erasure and pinpoint hosts where the payload actually executed. Rationale: The .pkg_history/.pkg_logs temp artifacts are named explicitly in the StepSecurity and Microsoft analyses as dropper leftovers; because the dropper self-deletes the payload, these marker files are the durable execution evidence and are extremely unlikely to occur benignly. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised-using-easy-day-js • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An unrelated tool coincidentally using a .pkg_history dotfile in temp (rare — validate the initiating process is node/npm)
  • IR analysts re-detonating the sample and regenerating the markers
  • A restored disk image from a compromised machine replaying the files without live execution
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is node/npm and check the file's parent folder for a recently-deleted .js payload (correlate with DeviceFileEvents ActionType=FileDeleted on the same host). 2) Contain: isolate the host and preserve the temp directory for forensics before wiping node_modules. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2 for C2 beacons and UC4 for browser/wallet data access on the same DeviceName to determine whether the infostealer stage ran and exfiltrated.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ (".pkg_history",".pkg_logs")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe","node")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ (".pkg_history",".pkg_logs")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","npm","pnpm","yarn")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: easy-day-js Dropper Temp Marker Files (.pkg_history/.pkg_logs)
id: b71e0c39-5a2d-4f6c-8e19-9d3a4c7f2e08
description: Detects the .pkg_history and .pkg_logs artifacts written by the self-deleting easy-day-js postinstall dropper.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised-using-easy-day-js
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/02
tags:
  - attack.t1070.004
  - attack.t1195.001
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\.pkg_history'
      - '\.pkg_logs'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:*\\.pkg_history OR @TargetFilename:*\\.pkg_logs)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/(\.pkg_history|\.pkg_logs)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name=".pkg_history" OR Filesystem.file_name=".pkg_logs") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.process_guid | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name=".pkg_history" OR Filesystem.file_name=".pkg_logs") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.process_guid | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
easy-day-js second-stage infostealer reading browser secrets & crypto-wallet extensions via node AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for a node process (the easy-day-js second-stage payload) accessing browser credential stores and cryptocurrency-wallet extension data. The recovered payload is a cross-platform infostealer targeting browser databases and 160+ wallet extensions, so node touching Chrome/Edge/Brave/Firefox 'Login Data'/'Local State' or wallet extension folders is a strong collection signal. Rationale: JFrog/Microsoft describe the recovered stage-2 as a Node-based cross-platform infostealer parsing browser databases and 160+ crypto-wallet extensions; node.exe reading Chrome/Edge 'Login Data'/'Local State' or Local Extension Settings is anomalous for a build tool and captures the collection stage this campaign is financially motivated to reach. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/easy-day-js/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Electron/VS Code or other node-based desktop apps legitimately reading their own Chromium 'Local State' profile
  • Browser-automation frameworks (Puppeteer/Playwright) driven by node accessing profile data during tests
  • A backup/sync agent implemented in node copying user profile directories
  • Password-manager browser-import tooling built on node
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Microsoft VS Code\" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("puppeteer","playwright","electron")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the node process lineage — a node spawned by npm/postinstall or from a temp .js path is malicious, whereas a signed Electron app path is likely benign; correlate the DeviceName with UC1/UC2 hits. 2) Contain: isolate the host and force-reset all browser-saved credentials and any crypto-wallet seed/keys for the affected user; revoke cloud/SSO sessions. 3) Hunt: check UC2 for outbound beacons to 23.254.164.123:443 (exfil channel) and review proxy logs for large POSTs from the host to confirm data left the environment.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where (FileName in~ ("Login Data","Local State","Cookies","Web Data"))
     or FolderPath has_any (@"\User Data\Default\Local Extension Settings", "Local Extension Settings", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\", @"\BraveSoftware\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\", @"\Chromium\")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Targets=make_set(FolderPath, 30) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| where (TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Local State","Cookies","Web Data")) or TargetFilePath has "Local Extension Settings"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("Google/Chrome","Microsoft/Edge","BraveSoftware","Mozilla/Firefox","Chromium",@"Google\Chrome",@"Microsoft\Edge")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Targets=make_set(TargetFilePath, 30) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by LastSeen desc
title: Node Process Reading Browser Secrets and Crypto Wallet Extensions (easy-day-js infostealer)
id: c4a8f1d6-2e73-4b90-9c15-6f0b8a2d3e77
description: Detects a node process accessing browser credential stores or wallet extension data, consistent with the easy-day-js second-stage infostealer.
references:
  - https://research.jfrog.com/post/easy-day-js/
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/02
tags:
  - attack.t1555.003
  - attack.t1005
logsource:
  category: file_access
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith: '\node.exe'
  selection_target:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\User Data\Default\Login Data'
      - '\User Data\Local State'
      - '\Local Extension Settings\'
  condition: selection_proc and selection_target
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe) (@TargetFilename:*\\Login\ Data OR @TargetFilename:*\\Local\ State OR @TargetFilename:*\\Local\ Extension\ Settings\\*)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo ContextImageFileName=/\\node\.exe$/i
| regex("(Login Data|Local State|Local Extension Settings|\\\\Mozilla\\\\Firefox\\\\Profiles)", field=TargetFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.process_name="node.exe" OR Filesystem.process_name="node") AND (Filesystem.file_name IN ("Login Data","Local State","Cookies","Web Data") OR Filesystem.file_path="*Local Extension Settings*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.process_name="node.exe" OR Filesystem.process_name="node") AND (Filesystem.file_name IN ("Login Data","Local State","Cookies","Web Data") OR Filesystem.file_path="*Local Extension Settings*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "b73de25c053c3225a077738a1fcbd9ca6966d7b3cd6f5494a30f0aa0eae55c7e", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Multiple @immobiliarelabs Backstage Plugins Compromised on npm

StepSecurity
2026-07-01 12 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Compromised versions run a malicious payload at npm install time through a binding.gyp node-gyp hook, harvesting credentials from sources like GitHub Actions secrets, cloud provider keys, and package registry tokens, while trying to persist in AI coding assistant configs. Static analysis of version 2.1.2 against the clean 2.1.1 release revealed a new 5 MB index.js and an added binding.gyp, both absent from earlier releases.

Phantom Gyp binding.gyp install-time payload execution (Miasma npm worm) AIInstallation High
Hunts the GYP command-expansion shell invocation that the Miasma/Phantom Gyp worm plants in binding.gyp to run the 5 MB index.js during node-gyp configure, bypassing scripts.postinstall monitoring. The exact source line is '<!(node index.js > /dev/null 2>&1 && echo stub.c)', so a process command line carrying both 'node index.js' and 'echo stub.c' is the worm firing. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim binding.gyp source string '<!(node index.js > /dev/null 2>&1 && echo stub.c)' from the article; the 'node index.js' + 'echo stub.c' pairing is unique to the Phantom Gyp configure-step trick and not a legitimate gyp pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://snyk.io/blog/node-gyp-supply-chain-compromise-self-propagating-npm-worm-binding-gyp/ • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate native addon packages whose binding.gyp uses node-based command expansion (rare; almost never invokes a bare index.js with echo stub.c)
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sandbox
  • CI job intentionally re-running the malicious tarball for analysis
  • A developer's own gyp build script that happens to echo a stub source file
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and the parent chain (npm/node-gyp/sh) and identify which @immobiliarelabs (or other) package was being installed; confirm a 5 MB index.js + binding.gyp exist in that package dir. 2) Contain: isolate the host/runner, revoke any tokens that were live in that session (GitHub, npm, cloud), and rotate CI secrets exposed to the job. 3) Hunt: search the same host for a Bun binary in temp, IMDS (169.254.169.254) hits, and writes to AI-assistant configs (.claude/settings.json etc.); pivot org-wide on the affected package@version.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_all ("node index.js", "echo stub.c")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_all ("node index.js", "echo stub.c")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
